In chapters 4 and 5 we computed the displacement of a bar and the deflection of a beam by integrating the equation of equilibrium. This worked because the loads and the shapes were simple. The hanging bar has a constant cross section and a load that is the same everywhere, the cantilever has a constant bending stiffness and one force. For a bar with a step in the middle the writing already gets complicated, for a beam whose cross section changes along its length and which carries many loads the integration becomes long, and for a body that is a machine part with holes we do not know how to write the true displacement at all. A computer must give displacements all the same. The question of the chapter is: how do we find an approximate displacement when we cannot write the true one, and how do we find out how good it is?

We have already seen an answer in a small way. For the hanging bar we chose the straight line \(c\,x\) in section 4.6.8 and looked for the number \(c\) at which the total potential energy is smallest. We got \(c = a L\), the displacement of the end was exact, 19,52 µm, at the middle of the bar the line gave 9,760 µm instead of 14,64 µm, and the energy was \(-293{,}27\) µJ instead of \(-391{,}03\) µJ. For the cantilever in section 5.11.6 the parabola \(a\,x^2\) gave the end of the beam as \(-5{,}979\) mm instead of \(-7{,}972\) mm, that is three quarters of the true value. Both times the energy came out higher than the true one, never lower, and both times there was only one free number. The idea of the chapter is to turn this trying into a method: the trial field gets as many free numbers as we like, and the numbers follow from equations that we write in advance and that a computer can solve. We also want to know whether an approximation with more numbers really approaches the true field and how fast.

The route is this. In the first section we write equilibrium in a form that asks less of the unknown function than an equation at every point, and we test this form on a bar, on a bar with a step, on a beam and on a body. Trial fields made of straight pieces have kinks, so in the second section we check what of the computation in chapters 3 and 4 remains for functions with kinks. In the third section we collect the mathematics we need for the equations for the free numbers: the scalar product, carried over from vectors to functions, and systems of linear equations that have exactly one solution. Then we write the first method, in which the free numbers are found from the smallest energy, and in the fifth section we say how good its approximation is and why it is the best among all fields of the same family. The sixth section shows a route that needs no energy, because it starts directly from the equation of equilibrium, and compares it with the first. The last section takes trial fields made of straight pieces, which can be spread as densely as we like along the bar. This choice is the beginning of the finite element method, which we develop in chapter 7.

6.1 Strong and weak form (močna in šibka oblika)

In chapter 4 we wrote the equilibrium of a bar in two ways. The first is an equation at every point of the bar, \(N' + q = 0\) (lemma 4.75). The second is an equality of integrals for every virtual displacement (theorem 4.76). Which of the two asks less of the unknown displacement? And what do we gain by asking less? We need the answer before we look for approximations: an approximate field is usually less smooth than the true one, and if the equation at every point does not admit it, we must write the problem differently. First we describe both forms for a bar and compare them on a bar with a step, then we do the same for a beam and for a body.

6.1.1 Boundary value problem of a bar (robni problem palice)

Take the bar from section 4.4.4. It lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed at \(x = 0\). Its modulus of elasticity and cross-sectional area determine the axial stiffness \(EA\), a positive continuous function of position, which is constant for a bar with a constant cross section. A distributed axial load \(q\) (definition 4.74) and a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) at the end \(x = L\) act on it. The axial force is \(N = EA\,u'\), because the stress is \(E\,u'\) and the cross section is \(A\) (section 4.6.1). Equilibrium of parts of the bar gave \(N' + q = 0\) and \(N(L) = F\), and the fixing gave \(u(0) = 0\). Let us write all three requirements as a task about the unknown function \(u\).

Definition 6.1 Strong form of a boundary value problem of a bar (močna oblika robnega problema palice)

The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed at \(x = 0\). Let the axial stiffness \(EA\) be a positive continuous function on \([0, L]\), the load \(q\) a continuous function on \([0, L]\) (definition 4.74) and \(F\) a number, the force at the end \(x = L\). The strong form (močna oblika) of the boundary value problem of a bar is the task: find a function \(u\) on \([0, L]\) that has a continuous derivative \(u'\) (one-sided at the ends), whose axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\) and which satisfies

\[\begin{aligned} &\big(EA\,u'\big)'(x) + q(x) = 0 \quad \text{for every } x \in (0, L) , \\ &u(0) = 0 , \qquad EA\,u'(L) = F . \end{aligned} \tag{6.1}\]

Such a statement, an equation at every interior point and conditions at the ends, is a boundary value problem (robni problem).

Source: EP §6.3.6.2 (p. 323, 326-327), COOK §4.7, (4.7-2) (PDF p. 166).

What does the definition say in words? At every point of the bar the derivative of the axial force must equal the negative of the load, so the axial force must change along the bar exactly as the load demands at every metre. For the axial force to have a derivative, the function \(u\) must have a second derivative if \(EA\) is constant. Besides the equation we have two conditions at the ends. The condition \(u(0) = 0\) prescribes a displacement and is an essential condition (bistveni pogoj), the condition \(EA\,u'(L) = N(L) = F\) prescribes a force and is a natural condition (naravni pogoj), as we distinguished them in section 4.4.7 and for the beam in section 5.11.4.

Let us test the definition on the hanging bar (section 4.6.8): \(L = 10\) m, \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N, \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m, \(F = 0\). These and all further numbers of the hanging bar are computed from unrounded data (\(E\), \(\rho\), \(g\) and \(A = \pi\,(5\ \text{mm})^2\)), as in chapter 4. With the rounded \(EA\) and \(q\) the last digit can differ: the energy of the true field is \(-391{,}03\) µJ, while the rounded data would give \(-391{,}16\) µJ. The true field \(u = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) has the axial force \(N = EA\,u' = 2a\,EA\,(L - x) = 6{,}010\ \text{N/m} \cdot (L - x)\), whose derivative is \(-6{,}010\) N/m \(= -q\), and \(N(L) = 0 = F\). It satisfies the strong form. The line \(u = c\,x\) from section 4.6.8, however, has the constant axial force \(N = EA\,c\), so the left side of equation (6.1) is \(0 + q = 6{,}010\) N/m at every point, whatever the number \(c\) is. The strong form of the line therefore does not distinguish better from worse, because the number \(c\) does not appear in it. No line satisfies it, and the measure of how much it fails tells us nothing about the number \(c\).

6.1.2 Weak form of a bar (šibka oblika palice)

Theorem 4.76 showed that the true displacement satisfies an equation with integrals over the bar in which only the first derivative of the displacement appears. This equation is equilibrium multiplied by a virtual displacement and integrated over the bar. Now let us take it as the definition of the task. We keep in mind that we shall assemble trial fields from pieces, so we allow functions with kinks (pregib), such as the field with a roof in section 1.15.5. The displacement of such a field is continuous, but its derivative may jump at finitely many points. The next section treats these functions exactly, here we say only what we need.

Definition 6.2 Weak form of a boundary value problem of a bar (šibka oblika robnega problema palice)

The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed at \(x = 0\). Let the axial stiffness \(EA\) (positive) and the load \(q\) be functions continuous piece by piece: there is a partition of the interval \([0, L]\) for which both are continuous on every closed piece, with one-sided values at the ends. Let the force at the end \(x = L\) be \(F\). An admissible function of a bar (dopustna funkcija palice) is a function \(w\) on \([0, L]\) that is continuous, satisfies \(w(0) = 0\), and for which there is a partition \(0 = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = L\) for which \(w\) is differentiable on every closed piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with a continuous derivative, one-sided at the ends. The derivative \(w'\) is thus determined everywhere except at the points of the partition, and the integral of a product with a function continuous on pieces means the sum of the integrals over the pieces. For several functions we take a partition that is common to all, adding to it the points of the partitions of the other functions. The weak form (šibka oblika) of the boundary value problem of a bar is the task: find an admissible function \(u\) that for every admissible function \(w\) satisfies

\[\int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L) . \tag{6.2}\]

The admissible function \(w\) is here called a test function (preizkusna funkcija).

Source: EP §6.3.6.2, (6.3.40) to (6.3.43) (p. 327), COOK §4.1 (PDF p. 150) and §4.7 (PDF p. 166), BOWER §8.1.2 (PDF p. 496). Summarized from theorem 4.76, the notation with pieces is not from the sources.

The test function is the virtual displacement from section 4.4: an imagined change of displacement that does not move the support (definition 4.70). The condition \(w(0) = 0\) is this constraint, just as for the bar. The function \(u\) in the task is an admissible function, so it satisfies the same condition and the same continuity as the test functions, but not the other equation. The weak form asks for a single derivative of the displacement, \(u'\), whereas the strong form also asks for the derivative of the axial force, that is \(u''\) for a constant stiffness. The natural condition \(EA\,u'(L) = F\) is built into the weak form: the term \(F\,w(L)\) stands right on the right side of equation (6.2). The essential condition \(u(0) = 0\) is not in the equation, because it is part of the set of admissible functions. Figure 6.1 compares the requirements: the strong form asks for equilibrium at every point, and the weak form for the equality of two areas formed by the test function. Figure 6.2 shows two test functions, a smooth one and one with a kink.

How are the forms related? If \(u\) is a solution of the strong form, it is a solution of the weak form. The converse holds under a condition that we state in the theorem, and from the weak form follow all the conditions of the strong one, even those that are not in its statement.

Theorem 6.3 Strong and weak form of a bar (močna in šibka oblika palice)

Let the bar, \(EA\), \(q\) and \(F\) be as in definition 6.2.

  1. Let \(EA\) and \(q\) be continuous on \([0, L]\). If \(u\) is a solution of the strong form (definition 6.1), then \(u\) is a solution of the weak form.
  2. Let \(u\) be a solution of the weak form and let there be a partition \(0 = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = L\) for which \(EA\) and \(q\) are continuous on every closed piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), \(u\) is differentiable on every piece with a continuous derivative, and on every piece the axial force \(EA\,u'\) equals a function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) that is continuously differentiable on the closed piece. Then:
    • (a) \(N_{\mathrm{k}}'(x) + q(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in [x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) and every \(k = 1, \dots, m\),
    • (b) \(N_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = N_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) for \(k = 1, \dots, m-1\), so the axial force is continuous across the points of the partition,
    • (c) \(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) = F\).
Proof

We must show two directions. The first is integration by parts on the pieces, the second reverses this step and from the equation for every test function chooses in turn functions that are nonzero only on one piece, at one junction and at the end.

1. The strong form implies the weak form.

  1. The derivative \(u'\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), so \(u\) is differentiable on \([0, L]\), one-sidedly at the ends, and therefore continuous (lemma 1.79). Together with \(u(0) = 0\) this is an admissible function with a partition of one piece.
  2. Let \(w\) be an admissible function with the partition \(0 = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = L\). By definition 6.1 the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\), and the field \(w\) is differentiable on every closed piece with a continuous derivative. By corollary 3.41 on integration by parts, on the piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) we have
    \[\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = N(x_{\mathrm{k}})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - N(x_{\mathrm{k}-1})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}-1}) - \int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  3. We add over \(k\). By the convention of definition 6.2, \(\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces, so it is the sum of the left sides. The function \(N'\,w = -q\,w\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), so the sum of the integrals \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\) equals \(\int_0^L N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\) by additivity of the integral (lemma 3.39, item 2). At the point \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(1 \le k \le m-1\) there appear the terms \(N(x_{\mathrm{k}})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) from piece \(k\) and \(-N(x_{\mathrm{k}})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) from piece \(k+1\). They are the same number, because \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous, so they cancel. What remains is
    \[\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = N(L)\,w(L) - N(0)\,w(0) - \int_0^L N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  4. Since \(w(0) = 0\), \(N(L) = F\) and \(N' = -q\) by equation (6.1), this is \(\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = F\,w(L) + \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\). Because \(N = EA\,u'\), this is equation (6.2).

2. The weak form implies the conditions.

  1. Let \(w\) be an admissible function. We refine the partition with the partition of the function \(w\). At the added points \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous, so their terms cancel in the summation, as in step 3 of the first direction. By corollary 3.41 on every piece and after summation we have
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x &= N_{\mathrm{m}}(L)\,w(L) \\ &\quad + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m-1} \big(N_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - N_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\big)\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \int_0^L N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x , \end{aligned}\]
    where \(N'\) on piece \(k\) is the derivative of the function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\), and the term at \(x = 0\) vanishes because of \(w(0) = 0\).
  2. Let us introduce \(J_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - N_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\), the jump of the axial force at the point \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\). We insert this into equation (6.2) and move all terms to the left side:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\big(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) - F\big)\,w(L) + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m-1} J_{\mathrm{k}}\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \int_0^L \big(N' + q\big)\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 \\ &\text{for every admissible function } w . \quad (*) \end{aligned}\]
  3. Let us choose a piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) and a function \(\psi\) that is differentiable on it with a continuous derivative and satisfies \(\psi(x_{\mathrm{k}-1}) = \psi(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\). The function \(w\) that equals \(\psi\) on this piece and zero elsewhere is continuous, zero at \(x = 0\) and differentiable with a continuous derivative on every closed piece of the partition, so it is admissible. It is also zero at all points of the partition. Equation \((*)\) therefore says \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} (N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q)\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for every such \(\psi\).
  4. The function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q\) is continuous on \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), because \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuously differentiable and \(q\) continuous on the piece. By the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (lemma 4.77) we therefore have \(N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q = 0\) on the whole piece. This is item (a).
  5. Now the integral in \((*)\) is zero for every admissible function \(w\), and what remains is \((N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) - F)\,w(L) + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} J_{\mathrm{k}}\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\).
  6. Let \(1 \le k \le m-1\) and \(0 < h < \min(x_{\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{k}-1},\, x_{\mathrm{k}+1} - x_{\mathrm{k}})\). The roof \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is zero to the left of \(x_{\mathrm{k}} - h\) and to the right of \(x_{\mathrm{k}} + h\), rises linearly to \(1\) at \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and falls linearly, is continuous, zero at \(0\) and \(L\), and differentiable with a continuous derivative on every piece of the partition refined by the points \(x_{\mathrm{k}} \pm h\). It is therefore admissible. Its value is \(1\) at \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(0\) at all other points of the partition, including \(L\). Step 5 gives \(J_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). This is item (b).
  7. The function \(w(x) = x\) with \(w(L) = L\) is also admissible. Since all \(J_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) by step 6, step 5 gives \((N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) - F)\,L = 0\) and therefore \(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) = F\). This is item (c).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The connection between the two forms for a smooth case is mentioned by EP §6.3.6.2 (pp. 323-328) and COOK §4.7 (PDF pp. 166-167), theorem 4.78 is the same conclusion for a continuously differentiable axial force.

What did the theorem show? The first direction is integration by parts, which moves the derivative from the axial force to the test function, as in theorem 4.76, except that we run it piece by piece also across the points where the test function has a kink. The second direction says more than it seems at first sight. From the single equation (6.2) for all admissible functions \(w\) we get the equation of equilibrium on every piece, the natural condition \(N(L) = F\) and the continuity of the axial force across every point where a piece ends. This continuity is not written in the equation, yet the equation demands it.

For the hanging bar with the line the difference now shows. The line \(u = c\,x\) is an admissible function. Into equation (6.2) we insert the test function \(w = x\) from figure 6.2. The left side is \(\int_0^L EA\,c\,\mathrm{d}x = EA\,c\,L\), the right side \(\int_0^L q\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = q\,L^2/2\), and the equality gives \(c = q\,L/(2EA) = a L = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). This is exactly the equation from step 4 of the first trial field in section 4.6.8. The strong form gave nothing, because the number \(c\) dropped out, and the weak form determined it, because it asked of the true field only an average, equilibrium with the weight \(w\). The line does not satisfy the equation for every test function, because it is not the true field. With \(w = x^2/(1\ \text{m})\), that is \(w' = 2x/(1\ \text{m})\) with \(x\) in metres, the left side is \(\int_0^L EA\,c\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = EA\,c\,L^2/(1\ \text{m}) = 3005\) N m, the right side \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = q\,L^3/3\,(1\ \text{m})^{-1} = 2003\) N m. The true field \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) gives on the left the same as on the right, \(2003\) N m. The line therefore satisfies the equation only for the chosen test function, not for all, and this is what we expect of it: a trial field with one free number satisfies one requirement. The idea that a trial field with \(n\) free numbers satisfies \(n\) requirements we develop in the following sections.

6.1.3 A bar with a step (palica s stopnico)

What happens if the cross section of a bar changes suddenly along its length? Take a steel hanging bar with an upper half, \(5\) m long, of diameter \(10\) mm and cross-sectional area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), and a lower half, \(5\) m long, of diameter \(5\) mm and area \(A/4 = 19{,}63\ \text{mm}^2\) (figure 6.3). The upper end is fixed, the lower end free, \(F = 0\), the only load is the weight. The material is the steel of the book (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3\), \(g = 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2\)). The load per unit length is \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m above and \(\rho g A/4 = 1{,}503\) N/m below. The step is a simplification: a real step would have a rounded transition, and the one-dimensional model does not capture the stress concentration next to it. We deal with it in chapter 11.

First let us find the true displacement by the method of chapter 4, piece by piece. Equilibrium of the part of the bar below a cross section (lemma 4.75) gives \(N(x) = \rho g\,(A/4)\,(10 - x)\) in the lower half, with \(x\) in metres, and \(N(x) = \rho g\,(A/4) \cdot 5 + \rho g A\,(5 - x)\) in the upper one. At \(x = 5\) m both expressions equal \(7{,}512\) N, so the axial force is continuous, and at \(x = 0\) we have \(N = 37{,}56\) N, the weight of the whole bar, \(5 \cdot 6{,}010 + 5 \cdot 1{,}503\) N. The strain \(u' = N/(EA)\) has the value \(4{,}880 \cdot 10^{-7}\) above the step and \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) below. They meet at the same point, but the derivative of the displacement jumps by a factor of \(4\), the ratio of the areas: the same force in a cross section four times thinner gives four times the elongation. We get the displacement from the integral of the strain: \(u(5\ \text{m}) = 7{,}320\) µm and \(u(10\ \text{m}) = 12{,}20\) µm. The graph of the displacement therefore has a kink at the point \(x = 5\) m and there is no second derivative there.

What does the strong form say about such a field? Its equation \((EA\,u')' + q = 0\) requires \(EA\) to be continuous (definition 6.1), but the axial stiffness jumps by a factor of \(4\) at the step. The load \(q\) also jumps, from \(6{,}010\) to \(1{,}503\) N/m, and so the axial force \(N' = -q\) does not have a continuous derivative across the step. This definition does not capture the true field. We would have to split the strong form into two parts and add two more conditions at the step: the displacement is continuous, the axial force is continuous. These two conditions are not written in the equation.

The weak form needs nothing extra. Let us test it. With \(w = x\) the left side of equation (6.2) is \(\int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x = 131{,}46\) N m, and the right side is \(\int_0^5 6{,}010\,x\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_5^{10} 1{,}503\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = 131{,}46\) N m. The equality also holds for the test function with a kink from figure 6.2, here with the kink at \(x = 5\) m, \(w = x\) up to \(5\) m and \(w = 5\) m afterwards: the left side is \(\int_0^5 N\,\mathrm{d}x = 112{,}68\) N m, the right side \(\int_0^5 6{,}010\,x\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_5^{10} 1{,}503 \cdot 5\,\mathrm{d}x = 112{,}68\) N m. The displacement of the bar with a step is therefore an admissible function and a solution of the weak form, even though its derivative is discontinuous. For every test function this follows from steps 2 to 4 of the first direction of the proof of theorem 6.3: we take the partition common with the point \(x = 5\) m, the axial force is continuous and \(N' = -q\) on every piece, and the terms at the step cancel. Theorem 6.3, item 2, says the converse: every solution of the weak form with piecewise smooth fields \(u\) and \(N\) has a continuous axial force and a continuous displacement at the step, even though we wrote this nowhere. The continuity of the displacement is in the definition of an admissible function, and the continuity of the axial force came out of the equation itself. This is the reason why the weak form also admits bars whose stiffness or load jumps.

6.1.4 Weak form of a beam (šibka oblika nosilca)

We put the same question to the beam from chapter 5. Let it lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) with bending stiffness \(EI\) and load \(q\), positive upward. The strong form is the equation of the deflection curve (theorem 5.42)

\[\big(EI\,v''\big)'' = q\]

with four conditions at the ends from section 5.7.2. At every end there is one condition from the pair \((v, V)\) and one from the pair \((v', M)\): essential if the support prescribes the deflection or the slope, natural if it prescribes the shear force or the moment (the table in section 5.11.4). For a constant stiffness \(v\) must have four derivatives.

We know the weak form from theorem 5.62: equilibrium multiplied by a virtual displacement and integrated by parts twice. For \(N = 0\) and \(M = EI\,v''\) what remains is

\[\begin{aligned} \int_0^L EI\,v''\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x &+ \Big[F_{\mathrm{y}}\,w + M_0\,w'\Big]_{\mathrm{x} = \mathrm{L}} \\ &+ \Big[F_{\mathrm{y}}\,w + M_0\,w'\Big]_{\mathrm{x} = 0} . \end{aligned} \tag{6.3}\]

Here \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M_0\) are the force across the axis and the moment of a couple at the ends (each end has its own values, the loads are positive upward and counterclockwise), and at every end we omit the terms of the components that the support forbids. The test functions \(w\) are the virtual displacements of a beam (definition 5.60): \(w\) and \(w'\) continuous, \(w''\) continuous (the next section allows \(w''\) to have jumps), and \(w = 0\) where \(v\) is prescribed and \(w' = 0\) where \(v'\) is prescribed. We proved the equivalence of the two forms in chapter 5: the weak one follows from the strong one by theorem 5.62, and the converse by theorem 5.65, which gives the equation \((EI\,v'')'' = q\) in the interior and the natural conditions \(V = F_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M = M_0\) at a free end. A point force or a couple in the interior adds a term by corollary 5.64. The natural conditions and the point forces are therefore in the weak form only terms on the right side.

Why is the continuity of the slope \(w'\) important here? The equation contains \(w''\), and if \(w'\) had a jump, such as a kink in the deflection, then \(w''\) at that point would not be a function. The term \(M_0\,w'\) at a free end is the work of the couple on the rotation of the end, which must be well defined. Later in this chapter we show with numbers that the energy of a rounded kink in the deflection grows beyond all bounds when we shorten the rounding.

Let us test equation (6.3) on the cantilever from section 5.1.3: \(L = 1\) m, force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -500\) N at the free end, \(M_0 = 0\), clamped at \(x = 0\). The moment is \(M = EI\,v'' = -500\ \text{N} \cdot (L - x)\). The test function must have \(w(0) = w'(0) = 0\), so \(w = x^2/(1\ \text{m})\) is one of the admissible ones, with \(x\) in metres, \(w'' = 2/(1\ \text{m})\) and \(w(L) = 1\) m. The left side is \(\int_0^L M\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = -500\ \text{N m}\), the right side \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\,w(L) + M_0\,w'(L) = -500\ \text{N} \cdot 1\ \text{m} = -500\ \text{N m}\). The equation holds. We do the same on the simply supported beam from section 5.1.3, \(L = 2\) m, \(q = -q_0\) with \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m, where \(M = \tfrac12\,q_0\,x\,(L - x)\). The test function \(w = x\,(L - x)/(1\ \text{m})\) is zero at both supports, and \(w'' = -2/(1\ \text{m})\). The left side is \(\int_0^L M\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = -1333{,}3\) N m, the right side \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = -1333{,}3\) N m, there are no terms at the ends, because \(w = 0\) everywhere there and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = M_0 = 0\).

The support says what the trial field must satisfy. A beam clamped at \(x = 0\) requires \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\). A simply supported beam requires \(v = 0\) at both supports, but the trial field does not require the moment \(M = 0\), because it is a natural condition and equation (6.3) satisfies it by itself when the field is the true one, as we saw in section 5.11.4.

6.1.5 Weak form of a body (šibka oblika telesa)

The last answer is for a body. Take the body from section 4.5.1: a set of points \(V\), the surface divided into a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) with prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) and a part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) with prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\), and the body force \(\vek b\). The strong form gathers what we established in chapters 1 to 3: the equilibrium equations \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} + b_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) in the interior, the condition \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the condition \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the stress from the strain by the general Hooke's law (definition 3.16) and the strain from the displacement (definition 1.115). The weak form is the equality of internal and external virtual work, equation (4.51), in which the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is expressed by the displacement \(\vek u\). The equivalence of the two forms is already proved. From the equilibrium equations and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the equation of virtual work follows by theorem 4.82, and from the equation of virtual work for every admissible virtual displacement the equilibrium equations and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) follow by theorem 4.84. The condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is built into the set of fields in both. The theorems hold under the assumptions of section 4.5.1: a body made of boxes, a continuously differentiable and symmetric stress. Plane states, in which two coordinates suffice, have the same form and we treat them in chapter 11.

The test function is here a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (figure 6.4). Let us test this on the cube of section 4.5.1, glued to the table, \(h = 10\) mm, \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\) everywhere. The virtual displacement \(\vek w = (\gamma\,z, 0, 0)\) with \(\gamma = 0{,}001\) is admissible, because it is zero at \(z = 0\) (section 4.5.2), and has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}(\vek w) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}(\vek w) = \gamma/2\), the other virtual strains are zero. The internal virtual work is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} (\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}})\,\gamma/2\,\mathrm{d}V = \tau_0\,\gamma\,h^3 = 0{,}0500\) N m. We neglect the weight, \(\vek b = \vek 0\), as in section 4.5.1. The external virtual work comes only from the top face with \(\bar{\vek t} = \tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), where \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = \gamma h\): \(\tau_0\,\gamma\,h \cdot h^2 = 0{,}0500\) N m. The front and the back face are free, \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). On the left and right faces the forces are vertical, \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and their work is zero, and the bottom face is \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), where \(\vek w = \vek 0\). The equality holds.

All three statements have the same form. On the left is an expression that is linear in the unknown field and in the test function at the same time, and on the right an expression that is linear only in the test function and contains the loads. Let us name them.

Definition 6.4 Bilinear form (bilinearna forma)

Let \(W\) be a vector space of functions or fields (definition 1.16). A bilinear form (bilinearna forma) on \(W\) is a function \(B\) that takes two elements \(u\) and \(w\) of the space \(W\) as input and gives one number \(B(u, w)\) as output, and is linear in each argument separately: \(B(\alpha u_1 + \beta u_2, w) = \alpha\,B(u_1, w) + \beta\,B(u_2, w)\) and \(B(u, \alpha w_1 + \beta w_2) = \alpha\,B(u, w_1) + \beta\,B(u, w_2)\) for all \(u, u_1, u_2, w, w_1, w_2 \in W\) and numbers \(\alpha, \beta\). It is symmetric (simetrična) if \(B(u, w) = B(w, u)\) for all \(u, w \in W\).

Source: EP §6.2.4 (pp. 281-282), (6.2.31).

Definition 6.5 Linear form (linearna forma)

Let \(W\) be a vector space of functions or fields. A linear form (linearna forma) on \(W\) is a function \(\ell\) that takes an element \(w\) of the space \(W\) as input and gives a number \(\ell(w)\) as output, and satisfies \(\ell(\alpha w_1 + \beta w_2) = \alpha\,\ell(w_1) + \beta\,\ell(w_2)\) for all \(w_1, w_2 \in W\) and numbers \(\alpha, \beta\).

Source: EP §6.2.4 (p. 281), §6.3.6.2, (6.3.42) (p. 327).

The notation \(\ell(w)\) with a function in brackets is a linear form. The letter \(\ell\) without an argument is in chapter 1 the arm of a lever and is something else. The three tasks that we have collected are, in these notations:

task \(B(u, w)\) \(\ell(w)\)
bar \(\int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L)\)
beam \(\int_0^L EI\,u''\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x\) \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + [F_{\mathrm{y}} w + M_0 w']_{\mathrm{x} = \mathrm{L}} + [F_{\mathrm{y}} w + M_0 w']_{\mathrm{x} = 0}\)
body \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k},\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}(\vek u)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek w)\,\mathrm{d}V\) \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}A\)

For a body \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}(\vek u)\) is the strain of the field \(\vek u\) (equation (1.51)), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek w)\) the strain of the test field \(\vek w\), which is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.79), and \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) the constants of the generalized Hooke's law (definition 3.16), so that \(\sum_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}(\vek u) = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Each of the three has the first argument linear because in every case the stress is linear in the displacement (section 3.2.5), and the second because the virtual strain and the virtual displacement appear linearly. Symmetry: for the bar and the beam the product of functions is symmetric, for the body \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) by theorem 3.47, item 1, and the change of the order of the arguments is an exchange of the indices of a pair. All three tasks therefore have the same form.

The weak form of all three is thus one sentence. Let us write it for every task with such forms, since further on we shall also use it for the bar fixed at both ends, for beams and for the body.

Definition 6.6 Weak form with a bilinear and a linear form (šibka oblika z bilinearno in linearno formo)

Let \(X\) be the vector space of fields among which the task seeks the solution, \(B\) a bilinear form and \(\ell\) a linear form on \(X\). For the bar \(X\) is the space of the continuous functions of definition 6.2 without the condition at the support, for the beam the space of functions with continuous \(w\), \(w'\) and \(w''\), for the body the space of continuously differentiable fields (definition 1.90). The essential conditions of the task prescribe the values of the field on the supported part of the boundary, for the beam possibly also of the slope. An admissible field (dopustno polje) is a field from \(X\) that satisfies the essential conditions. A test function is a field from \(X\) that is zero wherever the essential conditions prescribe something, for the beam together with the slope where this is prescribed. The sum and a multiple of test functions are again test functions, so they form a vector space \(W\). The weak form (šibka oblika) of the task is the task: find an admissible field \(u\) for which

\[B(u, w) = \ell(w) \qquad \text{for every } w \in W . \tag{6.4}\]

For the bar fixed at \(x = 0\) this is definition 6.2, for the beam equation (6.3) and for the body equation (4.51).

Source: EP (6.3.43) (p. 327), where the test function is the first argument of the form \(B\), which for a symmetric form is the same.

We shall need one more property all the time: that \(B(w, w)\) is not negative and is zero only for \(w = 0\). Why? \(B(w, w)\) is twice the strain energy of the field \(w\) (bar and beam: because the energy is \(\tfrac12\,EA\,w'^2\) or \(\tfrac12\,EI\,w''^2\) per unit length, body: equation (3.41)). The energy is positive if the bar really deforms. Zero energy, however, means that the bar or the body deforms nowhere, so it only moves as a rigid body, and the supports do not allow this.

Lemma 6.7 Positivity of the energy (pozitivnost energije)

Let \(B\) be the bilinear form of one of the three tasks in the table and \(W\) the space of its test functions (definition 6.6), and let \(B(w, w) = 2U(w)\) be twice the strain energy of the field \(w\). Then \(B(w, w) \ge 0\) for every \(w \in W\), and \(B(w, w) = 0\) only for \(w = 0\), if the assumptions of the task hold:

  1. bar: \(EA > 0\) continuous on pieces, the bar fixed at least at one end,
  2. beam: \(EI > 0\) continuous, \(w\) and \(w'\) continuous, \(w''\) continuous, and the only straight line \(w = \alpha + \beta x\) in \(W\) is \(w = 0\) (for example for the clamp \(w(0) = w'(0) = 0\) or for the supports \(w(0) = w(L) = 0\)),
  3. body of isotropic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\), a connected interior of the body, and the only rigid motion \(\vek w = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) (constant vector \(\vek a\), antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\)) that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is \(\vek w = \vek 0\).
Proof

We must show non-negativity, and then in each case that zero energy implies the zero field.

  1. Bar. The integrand \(EA\,w'^2\) is not negative, so the integral over every piece is not negative either (lemma 3.39, item 4). Let the sum of the integrals over the pieces be zero. Since none is negative, each is zero. Suppose that \(w'(x_0) \ne 0\) at some point of a piece. Then the function \(EA\,w'^2\) is continuous on the piece and positive at \(x_0\), and as in steps 6 and 7 of the proof of corollary 4.93 the integral over a neighbourhood of \(x_0\) has a positive lower bound, a contradiction. Therefore \(w' = 0\) on every piece, by corollary 1.85 \(w\) is constant on every piece, and since it is continuous, it is constant on the whole \([0, L]\). A test function is zero at the fixed end, so \(w = 0\).
  2. Beam. The same argument with \(EI\,w''^2\) gives \(w'' = 0\) on \([0, L]\). By corollary 1.85 \(w'\) is constant, \(w' = \beta\), and \(w - \beta x\) has derivative zero, so \(w = \alpha + \beta x\). This line is in \(W\), so by assumption \(w = 0\).
  3. Body. By theorem 3.48, item 1, the strain energy density is positive for every strain that is not zero, and by theorem 3.47, item 2, \(B(w, w) = 2\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\,\mathrm{d}V\), where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\) is the strain energy density (definition 3.44) for the strain of the field \(\vek w\), so \(B(w, w) \ge 0\). Let \(B(w, w) = 0\). The density \(\Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\) is continuous and non-negative, so by the same argument as for the bar it is zero at every point of the interior, so the strain is zero at every point. By theorem 1.134 we have \(\vek w = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) on the interior, and by continuity on the whole body. The field is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so by assumption \(\vek w = \vek 0\).

Source: EP §6.2.5 (pp. 283, 287). The proof is not from a source, the bar we treated in steps 6 to 8 of the proof of corollary 4.93.

The assumption about the supports is not empty. The cube of section 4.5.1 is glued with its bottom face to the table, and there \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the face \(z = 0\). If \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r = \vek 0\) at the points \((0, 0, 0)\), \((h, 0, 0)\) and \((0, h, 0)\), then \(\vek a = \vek 0\), \(\mat W\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek 0\). An antisymmetric matrix with zero first two columns has, because of antisymmetry, zero first two rows as well, and its element \(W_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is zero, because the diagonal of an antisymmetric matrix is zero. So \(\mat W = \mat 0\) and the cube is held. The hanging bar as a body in section 4.5.1, however, has \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) empty, and the energy is zero for a rigid motion. The bar in this section has a fixed end \(u(0) = 0\) and the lemma holds for it.

The existence of a solution of the weak form for a bar and a beam is guaranteed by integration, as we did it in chapters 4 and 5. For a body the proof of existence is outside our computation. It needs the continuity of the bilinear form and the positivity that the lemma gave, and we leave it to chapter 11 (BATHE §4.3.4, PDF pp. 254-255). The statements about the body in this chapter are therefore written with the words "if a solution exists".

The weak form has a close connection with the total potential energy. The energy of the field \(u\) is \(\Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,B(u, u) - \ell(u)\), for the bar equation (4.62). Its difference between the fields \(u + \alpha w\) and \(u\) is \(\alpha\,\big(B(u, w) - \ell(w)\big) + \tfrac12\,\alpha^2\,B(w, w)\), which follows from bilinearity and symmetry. The term with \(\alpha\) is zero exactly when the weak form holds for \(w\). The weak form is therefore the condition that the energy changes, under a displacement in the direction of every test function, only by the term with \(\alpha^2\), and since the lemma on positivity says that this term is positive, the field is then the lowest among all admissible ones. We use this connection in the section where we find the free numbers from the smallest energy.

6.2 Mathematics: functions with kinks

The displacement of the stepped bar (section 6.1.3) has a kink. At \(x = 5\) m the stiffness \(EA\) changes abruptly by a factor of \(4\), while the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is continuous there, so the derivative \(u'\) must jump. Such a displacement has no second derivative and not even a derivative at every point. The trial fields of the finite element method (chapter 7) will be built from straight pieces that meet in kinks, so a kink is not a rare exception but the general rule. Chapter 4, however, proved the principle of virtual displacements and the principle of minimum energy for a bar for fields whose derivative is continuous on the whole bar. Do the two theorems stay true when the derivative jumps?

The answer is yes and it is short, because we cut the integral into pieces. First we say what a function that we differentiate piece by piece is and what its integral is. Then we prove the fundamental theorem of calculus and integration by parts for such functions, and at the end we repeat the proofs of chapter 4 for the bar and of chapter 5 for the beam. The general mathematical setting, in which all this is written without pieces, we only name.

6.2.1 Piecewise continuously differentiable functions

We met a field with kinks in section 1.15.5: the graph breaks along a line and the derivative does not exist there. For a function of one variable a kink is a point where the graph breaks and has different slopes to the left and to the right of it. Away from the kinks the function is smooth. So we describe it piece by piece. First we describe functions that are continuous piece by piece, then those that are continuously differentiable piece by piece.

Definition 6.8 Piecewise continuous function (odsekoma zvezna funkcija)

Let \([a, b]\) be a closed interval. A function \(f\), which takes a number \(x\) as input and gives the number \(f(x)\) as output, is piecewise continuous (odsekoma zvezna) on \([a, b]\) if there is a partition of the interval (definition 3.31) \(a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = b\) and for each \(k = 1, \dots, m\) a function \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\), continuous on the closed interval \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), such that \(f(x) = f_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\) for every \(x\) in the open interval \((x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}})\). The points \(x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{m}-1}\) are called break points (delilne točke).

Source: KREYSZIG §6.1 (PDF p. 235): a function is piecewise continuous if the interval can be divided into finitely many subintervals, on each of which the function is continuous and has finite limits as the endpoints are approached from the interior. The notation with the functions \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) is ours.

The function \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) is determined by \(f\), since its values at the ends of the piece are the limits of the values of \(f\) as the end is approached from inside the piece (lemma 1.80). The values of \(f\) at the break points do not interest us, so we may leave them undefined. If a function is piecewise continuous with some partition, it is piecewise continuous with every finer partition too, since we only restrict the functions \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) to subintervals. For finitely many piecewise continuous functions there is therefore a common partition, whose break points are the union of the break points of all of them. We will always take such functions on a common partition.

A piecewise continuous function is integrable on every piece, because it is continuous there (theorem 3.38). The integral over the whole interval is therefore the sum of the integrals over the pieces.

Definition 6.9 Integral of a piecewise continuous function (integral odsekoma zvezne funkcije)

Let \(f\) be a piecewise continuous function on \([a, b]\) with the partition \(a = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = b\) and the functions \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) of definition 6.8. Its integral (integral) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} f_{\mathrm{k}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{6.5}\]

where each term is the Riemann integral of a continuous function (definition 3.34). That the number does not depend on the choice of the partition is shown by item 1 of the next lemma.

Source: The definition is ours, since the books only use integrals of piecewise continuous functions. For a continuous function the partition may be just \(x_0 = a\), \(x_1 = b\) and the definition gives the integral of definition 3.34.

Lemma 6.10 Properties of the integral of piecewise continuous functions (lastnosti integrala odsekoma zveznih funkcij)

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be piecewise continuous functions on \([a, b]\) and \(\alpha\) a real number.

  1. The integral does not depend on the partition: if two partitions are given with which \(f\) is piecewise continuous, equation (6.5) gives the same number for both.
  2. Linearity: \(\displaystyle\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b g\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\displaystyle\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \alpha f\,\mathrm{d}x = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. Nonnegativity: if on a common partition \(f_{\mathrm{k}}(x) \ge 0\) for every \(x \in [x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) and every \(k\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\). If in addition the integral is zero, then \(f_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) on every closed piece.
Proof

We must show three items. The first and the second follow from additivity and linearity of the integral on a piece, the third is an argument from the proof of corollary 4.93, written for a piece.

1. Independence of the partition.

  1. Let \(c\) be a point of the open piece \((x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}})\). By additivity (lemma 3.39, item 2), \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} f_{\mathrm{k}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{c} f_{\mathrm{k}} + \int_{\mathrm{c}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} f_{\mathrm{k}}\). So the sum over pieces does not change when a break point is added.
  2. Two given partitions \(D\) and \(D'\) have a common finer partition, obtained by uniting their points. We reach it from \(D\) by adding finitely many points and likewise from \(D'\). On a piece of the common partition the functions given by \(D\) and \(D'\) are equal: both are continuous on the closed piece and equal to \(f\) on the open piece, so they agree at the ends too (as for the function \(f_{\mathrm{k}}\) above). By step 1, \(D\) and \(D'\) give the same sum as the common partition.

2. Linearity.

  1. We take the common partition of the functions \(f\) and \(g\). On every closed piece \(f_{\mathrm{k}} + g_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\alpha f_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuous (corollary 1.64) and equal to \(f + g\) and \(\alpha f\) on the open piece. By linearity of the integral on a piece (lemma 3.39, item 1) the equality holds on every piece. We sum over the pieces.

3. Nonnegativity.

  1. By monotonicity on a piece (lemma 3.39, item 4, with the zero function) every term of the sum is nonnegative, hence so is the sum.
  2. Let the sum be zero. Since every term is nonnegative, every term is zero. Suppose that \(f_{\mathrm{k}}(x_0) > 0\) at some point \(x_0 \in [x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\). By continuity (definition 1.58) with the allowed error \(f_{\mathrm{k}}(x_0)/2\) there is a closed interval \([c, d] \subseteq [x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with \(c < d\), which contains \(x_0\) and on which \(f_{\mathrm{k}} > f_{\mathrm{k}}(x_0)/2\).
  3. By additivity the integral over the piece is the sum of the integrals over \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, c]\), \([c, d]\) and \([d, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) (if \(c = x_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) or \(d = x_{\mathrm{k}}\), the corresponding term drops out, because the integral over an interval of length zero is zero). The first and the third are not negative by step 4, and the middle one is by the bound (lemma 3.39, item 3) not smaller than \(\tfrac12 f_{\mathrm{k}}(x_0)\,(d - c) > 0\). This contradicts the integral over the piece being zero. So \(f_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. Item 3 is the same argument as in steps 6 and 7 of the proof of corollary 4.93.

Now we can say what a function is that we may differentiate piece by piece.

Definition 6.11 Piecewise continuously differentiable function (odsekoma zvezno odvedljiva funkcija)

Let \([a, b]\) be a closed interval. A function \(u\), which takes a number \(x\) as input and gives the number \(u(x)\) as output, is piecewise continuously differentiable (odsekoma zvezno odvedljiva) on \([a, b]\) if:

  1. \(u\) is continuous on \([a, b]\),
  2. there is a partition \(a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = b\), and on every open piece \((x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}})\) the function \(u\) is differentiable and its derivative \(u'\) is there equal to a function \(g_{\mathrm{k}}\), continuous on the closed piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\).

The derivative \(u'\) is defined everywhere except at the break points and is a piecewise continuous function by definition 6.8. At a break point \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) the function \(u\) has the left derivative \(g_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) and the right derivative \(g_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\), which may be different.

Source: The definition is ours, we met a kink in section 1.15.5. KREYSZIG §6.1 (PDF p. 235) has only piecewise continuous functions, not their derivatives.

Requirement 1 is essential: a function that jumps at a break point is not piecewise continuously differentiable, because the derivative on the pieces does not register the jump (the example in the remark below lemma 6.12). A function we know from chapter 4, that is a function differentiable at every point of the interval with a continuous derivative, is piecewise continuously differentiable with a single partition, \(m = 1\). The stepped bar is the first example with two pieces.

Definition 6.2 writes the same class differently, with a function that is differentiable on every closed piece with a continuous derivative, one-sided at the ends. The two classes are equal. Let \(u\) be piecewise continuously differentiable and \(x\) a point of the piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) to the left of \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\). By the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) \(\big(u(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - u(x)\big)/(x_{\mathrm{k}} - x) = g_{\mathrm{k}}(\xi)\) for some \(\xi\) between \(x\) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\). As \(x\) tends to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\xi\) tends to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{k}}(\xi)\) to \(g_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\), because \(g_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuous. The left derivative of \(u\) at \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is therefore \(g_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\), likewise the right derivative at \(x_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) is \(g_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}-1})\), so \(u\) is differentiable on the closed piece with the continuous derivative \(g_{\mathrm{k}}\). Conversely, a function of definition 6.2 satisfies both items of the definition, with \(g_{\mathrm{k}}\) its derivative on the closed piece. The admissible functions of a bar are therefore exactly the piecewise continuously differentiable functions \(w\) with \(w(0) = 0\).

The stepped bar (section 6.1.3): the upper \(5\) m have a diameter of \(10\) mm, the cross-sectional area is \(A\), and the lower \(5\) m have a diameter of \(5\) mm and area \(A/4\). It hangs under its own weight, fixed at the top. The axial force is \(N(5) = 7{,}512\) N on both sides of the step, because it is the weight of the lower part. The derivative of the displacement \(u' = N/EA\) is therefore at \(x = 5\) m \(4{,}880 \cdot 10^{-7}\) from above and \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) from below, four times larger, because \(EA\) below is four times smaller. The displacement is continuous, \(u(5) = 7{,}320\) µm from both sides, but its derivative is not. This is a piecewise continuously differentiable function with the partition \(0, 5, 10\), \(g_1 = N/(EA)\) on the upper piece and \(g_2 = N/(E A/4)\) on the lower one.

The simplest example of a kink is a function \(w\) in the shape of a roof on an interval with points \(x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < x_3\), which is zero at \(x_0\) and from \(x_2\) on, has the value \(1\) at \(x_1\) and is a straight line between these points (figure 6.5). The points are equally spaced, \(x_1 - x_0 = x_2 - x_1 = 3/2\), so the slopes are \(2/3\) and \(-2/3\). The derivative is constant on three pieces, \(2/3\), \(-2/3\) and \(0\), and at the break points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) it jumps by \(-4/3\) and \(2/3\). Such a function is the basic building block of trial fields made of straight pieces, which we will use in the rest of the chapter and in chapter 7.

The first theorem of analysis that we need is the fundamental theorem. It says that for a piecewise continuously differentiable function the values at the break points cancel when we sum over the pieces.

Lemma 6.12 Fundamental theorem of calculus for a function with kinks (osnovni izrek analize za funkcijo s pregibi)

Let \(u\) be a piecewise continuously differentiable function on \([a, b]\). Then

\[u(b) - u(a) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b u'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{6.6}\]
Proof

We must show that the differences of the values of the function \(u\) over the pieces add up to the difference over the whole interval. On every piece we use the fundamental theorem of calculus, and the intermediate values cancel because \(u\) is continuous.

  1. Let \(x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}}\) be the break points of definition 6.11. On the piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) the function \(u\) is continuous (item 1 of the definition), differentiable at every point of the open piece, and its derivative there equals the continuous function \(g_{\mathrm{k}}\) on the closed piece (item 2).
  2. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, item 1, with \(G = u\) and \(f = g_{\mathrm{k}}\) on the piece) \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} g_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mathrm{d}x = u(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - u(x_{\mathrm{k}-1})\).
  3. We sum over \(k = 1, \dots, m\). By equation (6.5) the left side is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b u'\,\mathrm{d}x\). On the right every intermediate term \(u(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) appears twice, once with a plus sign as the end of piece \(k\) and once with a minus sign as the beginning of piece \(k+1\). Since \(u\) is continuous, both values are the same number. What remains is \(u(x_{\mathrm{m}}) - u(x_0) = u(b) - u(a)\) (figure 6.6).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The statement is LEBL1 exercise 5.3.3 (PDF p. 205), there for a function that is differentiable everywhere except at finitely many points. The fundamental theorem is theorem 3.40 of chapter 3.

Let us test the theorem on the stepped bar. The increments over the pieces are \(\int_0^5 u'\,\mathrm{d}x = 7{,}320\) µm and \(\int_5^{10} u'\,\mathrm{d}x = 4{,}880\) µm, and their sum is \(12{,}20\) µm, which is exactly \(u(10) - u(0)\), because \(u(0) = 0\). Piece by piece it is the same computation as in section 6.1.3.

The continuity of \(u\) is necessary in step 3. The function that is \(0\) on \([0, 1/2]\) and \(1\) on \((1/2, 1]\) has derivative zero wherever it is differentiable, so \(\int_0^1 u'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\), while \(u(1) - u(0) = 1\). The jump of the function disappears, because the derivative on the pieces does not see it.

From the fundamental theorem follows integration by parts, which we need for the theorem on virtual displacements.

Lemma 6.13 Integration by parts for functions with kinks (integracija po delih za funkcije s pregibi)

Let \(N\) and \(w\) be piecewise continuously differentiable functions on \([a, b]\) on a common partition. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b N(x)\,w'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = N(b)\,w(b) - N(a)\,w(a) - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b N'(x)\,w(x)\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{6.7}\]
Proof

We must show that the two integrals differ by the difference of the product \(N w\) at the ends. The product is again piecewise continuously differentiable, so we use lemma 6.12.

  1. Let \(G = N w\) on \([a, b]\). The functions \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous by item 1 of definition 6.11, so their product is continuous too (corollary 1.64).
  2. On the open piece \((x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}})\) the functions \(N\) and \(w\) are differentiable, so by the product rule (lemma 1.81, item 3) \(G' = N'\,w + N\,w'\). On the closed piece the right side equals the continuous function \(g_{\mathrm{k}}^{N}\,w + N\,g_{\mathrm{k}}^{w}\), where \(g_{\mathrm{k}}^N\) and \(g_{\mathrm{k}}^w\) are the continuous functions of the definition for \(N\) and \(w\), and a product and a sum of continuous functions are continuous (corollary 1.64). So the function \(G\) is piecewise continuously differentiable.
  3. By lemma 6.12, \(G(b) - G(a) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (N'\,w + N\,w')\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  4. By linearity (lemma 6.10, item 2) the right side is the sum of the integrals \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b N'\,w\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b N\,w'\). We subtract the first on both sides and obtain equation (6.7).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The same theorem without kinks is corollary 3.41 of chapter 3 (LEBL1 exercise 5.3.5, PDF p. 205).

What did the lemma show? Along every piece integration by parts works as before, and the terms at the break points cancel in the sum if \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous at the break point. Let us test this on the hanging bar of chapter 3: \(L = 10\) m, \(\rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m, axial force \(N(x) = \rho g A\,(L - x)\) and a function \(w\) in the shape of a roof with a peak of \(1\) mm at the middle, which is \(0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) and a straight line between these points (partition \(0, 5, 10\) m). The derivative is \(w' = 2 \cdot 10^{-4}\) on the upper half and \(-2 \cdot 10^{-4}\) on the lower, \(N' = -\rho g A\). The left side is

\[\begin{aligned} \int_0^{L} N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x &= 2 \cdot 10^{-4} \Big(\int_0^{5} N\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_5^{10} N\,\mathrm{d}x\Big) \\ &= 2 \cdot 10^{-4}\,(225{,}4 - 75{,}1)\ \text{N m} = 0{,}03005\ \text{N m} . \end{aligned}\]

The right side is \(N(L)\,w(L) - N(0)\,w(0) - \int_0^{L} N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 - 0 + \rho g A \int_0^{L} w\,\mathrm{d}x = 6{,}010 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{N m} = 0{,}03005\ \text{N m}\), because the area of the triangle under the graph of \(w\) is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 10\ \text{m} \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 5 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2\). The two sides are equal. The terms at the ends are zero because \(w(0) = w(L) = 0\), and the term at the break point \(x = 5\) m cancels because \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous there.

What would happen if \(N\) were discontinuous at the break point? Take without units \(a = 0\), \(b = 1\), \(N = 2\) on \([0, \tfrac12]\) and \(N = 1\) on \((\tfrac12, 1]\), and a function \(w\) in the shape of a roof with a peak of \(1\) at \(x = \tfrac12\). The derivative is \(w' = 2\) on the left half and \(-2\) on the right. The left side is \(2 \cdot 2 \cdot \tfrac12 + 1 \cdot (-2) \cdot \tfrac12 = 1\). On the right \(N'= 0\) on the pieces and \(w(0) = w(1) = 0\), so \(0\). The difference is \(1 = (2 - 1) \cdot w(\tfrac12)\), the jump of the function \(N\) at the break point times the value of \(w\) there. In step 1 of the proof of the lemma a continuous product is therefore required: at a jump of \(N\) the function \(G\) would jump and lemma 6.12 would not hold. This is the reason why the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) of the stepped bar must be continuous across the step, even though \(u'\) is discontinuous.

6.2.2 The principle of minimum energy with kinks

Now we have the tool to repeat the proofs of chapter 4, that is theorem 4.76 on virtual displacements and corollary 4.93 on the minimum energy of a bar, for functions with kinks. The difference is twofold. The trial fields may have kinks, and the stiffness \(EA\) may be piecewise constant or piecewise continuous, as in the stepped bar. The continuity of the axial force across the break points is an assumption of the theorem, which equilibrium requires as well: a piece of the bar that encloses the step, with negligible weight on it, is in equilibrium only if the axial force on both sides is the same.

We do the same for the beam, where we have the same problem: for a beam \(EI\) may jump, and so the curvature \(v''\) jumps, while the moment \(M = EI\,v''\) is continuous. The trial fields of a beam may have kinks of the second kind: \(v\) and \(v'\) are continuous and \(v''\) jumps (why \(v'\) must not jump is explained in the paragraph after the proof).

Corollary 6.14 Virtual displacements and minimum energy with kinks (virtualni pomiki in najmanjša energija s pregibi)

Bar. The bar lies along the \(x\) axis from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed at \(x = 0\), as in theorem 4.76. Let the stiffness \(EA\) be piecewise continuous and positive on every closed piece, the axial load \(q\) piecewise continuous, and at the end \(x = L\) let a force \(F\) act in the direction of the axis, all independent of the deformation. An admissible field is an admissible function of a bar of the weak form (definition 6.2), that is a piecewise continuously differentiable function \(u\) on \([0, L]\) with \(u(0) = 0\) (definition 6.11). For an admissible field let

\[\Pi(u) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,u'^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,u\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,u(L) , \tag{6.8}\]

with the integrals of definition 6.9. Let \(u\) be an admissible field for which the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) (on the open pieces) is a piecewise continuously differentiable function, continuous on \([0, L]\), with \(N' + q = 0\) on the open pieces and \(N(L) = F\). Then:

  1. for every admissible field \(\delta u\), \(\displaystyle\int_0^L N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,\delta u\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L)\),
  2. for every admissible field \(\tilde u\), \(\displaystyle\Pi(\tilde u) - \Pi(u) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,(\tilde u' - u')^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\), with equality only for \(\tilde u = u\).

Beam. The beam lies along the \(x\) axis from \(0\) to \(L\) in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane with a piecewise continuous and positive stiffness \(EI\) and a piecewise continuous load \(q\) across the axis, signs as in chapter 5. An admissible field is a function \(v\) for which \(v\) and \(v'\) are continuous on \([0, L]\), \(v'\) is piecewise continuously differentiable and \(v\) satisfies the essential conditions of the supports. Let \(v\) be an admissible field for which \(M = EI\,v''\) and \(V\) are continuous on \([0, L]\) and piecewise continuously differentiable, with \(V' + q = 0\) and \(M' + V = 0\) on the open pieces, and at every end one of the possibilities holds: the support prohibits the corresponding component (\(v\) or \(v'\)), or the prescribed load equals the internal force, so at the end \(x = L\) we have \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = V(L)\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{L}} = M(L)\), and at the end \(x = 0\) we have \(f_0 = -V(0)\) and \(\mu_0 = -M(0)\). Then:

  1. for every admissible field \(\delta v\), \(\displaystyle\int_0^L M\,\delta v''\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,\delta v\,\mathrm{d}x + \Big[V\,\delta v + M\,\delta v'\Big]_0^L\), and the last term is the work of the loads at the ends, where the support does not prohibit the corresponding component,
  2. for \(\Pi(v) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EI\,v''^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,v\,\mathrm{d}x - f_0\,v(0) - \mu_0\,v'(0) - f_{\mathrm{L}}\,v(L) - \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\,v'(L)\) and every admissible field \(\tilde v\), \(\displaystyle\Pi(\tilde v) - \Pi(v) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EI\,(\tilde v'' - v'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\), if the only admissible variation of the form \(a + b\,x\) is the zero function (the supports exclude a rigid motion). Equality holds only for \(\tilde v = v\).
Proof

We must show four items. Items 1 and 3 are the proofs of theorems 4.76 and 5.62, in which lemma 6.12 replaces the fundamental theorem, and items 2 and 4 are the decomposition of corollaries 4.93 and 5.74, in which the integral of a square that is zero is handled by item 3 of lemma 6.10.

1. Virtual displacements of the bar.

  1. Let \(G = N\,\delta u\) on \([0, L]\). The functions \(N\) and \(\delta u\) are continuous, so the product \(G\) is continuous too (corollary 1.64). On the open pieces, by the product rule and because \(N' = -q\), \(G' = N'\,\delta u + N\,\delta u' = -q\,\delta u + N\,\delta u'\), which is a continuous function on the closed piece. The function \(G\) is therefore piecewise continuously differentiable, as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 6.13.
  2. By lemma 6.12 and linearity (lemma 6.10, item 2) \(\int_0^L (N\,\delta u' - q\,\delta u)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(L) - G(0)\). The value \(G(0)\) is zero, because \(\delta u(0) = 0\), and \(G(L) = F\,\delta u(L)\), because \(N(L) = F\). This is item 1.

2. Minimum energy of the bar.

  1. Let \(w = \tilde u - u\). This function is piecewise continuously differentiable on a common partition, \(w(0) = 0\) and \(w' = \tilde u' - u'\) on the open pieces (rules of differentiation, lemma 1.81, items 1 and 2). So it is an admissible field.
  2. As in steps 2 and 3 of the proof of corollary 4.93 we expand \(\tfrac12\,EA\,\tilde u'^2 = \tfrac12\,EA\,u'^2 + N\,w' + \tfrac12\,EA\,w'^2\) and with linearity of the integral we obtain
    \[\Pi(\tilde u) = \Pi(u) + \Big[\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,w(L)\Big] + \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,w'^2\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  3. The square bracket is zero by item 1 with \(\delta u = w\).
  4. The function \(\tfrac12\,EA_{\mathrm{k}}\,(g_{\mathrm{k}}^{w})^2\) is continuous and nonnegative on every closed piece, so by item 3 of lemma 6.10 the last integral is nonnegative. This is the equation of item 2.
  5. Let the last integral be zero. By the same item \(\tfrac12\,EA_{\mathrm{k}}\,(g_{\mathrm{k}}^{w})^2 = 0\) on every closed piece, because \(EA_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\), so \(w' = 0\) on every open piece. By corollary 1.85 (\(w\) is continuous on the closed piece and differentiable on the open one) \(w\) is constant on every piece. Neighbouring pieces share a break point, at which \(w\) is continuous, so they have the same constant, and \(w(x) = w(0) = 0\) everywhere. Hence \(\tilde u = u\).

3. Virtual displacements of the beam.

  1. Let \(G = V\,\delta v + M\,\delta v'\) on \([0, L]\). The functions \(V\), \(M\), \(\delta v\) and \(\delta v'\) are continuous, so \(G\) is continuous too. On an open piece \(G' = V'\,\delta v + V\,\delta v' + M'\,\delta v' + M\,\delta v''\), and with \(V' = -q\) and \(M' = -V\) the terms \(V\,\delta v'\) and \(M'\,\delta v' = -V\,\delta v'\) cancel: \(G' = -q\,\delta v + M\,\delta v''\). This is a continuous function on the closed piece, so \(G\) is piecewise continuously differentiable.
  2. By lemma 6.12 \(\int_0^L (M\,\delta v'' - q\,\delta v)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(L) - G(0)\), which is item 3. That this is the work of the end loads, where the support does not prohibit the component, follows from the end conditions as in step 5 of the proof of theorem 5.62: at the end \(x = L\) we have \(V\,\delta v + M\,\delta v' = f_{\mathrm{L}}\,\delta v + \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\,\delta v'\), at the end \(x = 0\) we have \(-G(0) = f_0\,\delta v + \mu_0\,\delta v'\), and the term of a component that the support prohibits is zero.

4. Minimum energy of the beam.

  1. Let \(w = \tilde v - v\). Both fields satisfy the same essential condition, so \(w\) is zero where the support prohibits \(v\) or \(v'\). So it is an admissible field.
  2. As in step 2 of the proof of corollary 5.74, \(\tfrac12\,EI\,\tilde v''^2 = \tfrac12\,EI\,v''^2 + M\,w'' + \tfrac12\,EI\,w''^2\), and with linearity \(\Pi(\tilde v) = \Pi(v) + [\int_0^L M\,w'' - \int_0^L q\,w - f_0\,w(0) - \mu_0\,w'(0) - f_{\mathrm{L}}\,w(L) - \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\,w'(L)] + \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EI\,w''^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. The square bracket is zero: by item 3 with \(\delta v = w\), \(\int_0^L M\,w'' - \int_0^L q\,w = [V\,w + M\,w']_0^L\), and every term at the ends cancels with the corresponding term in the bracket (by the end conditions), or is zero because \(w\) or \(w'\) is zero there.
  4. The last integral is nonnegative by item 3 of lemma 6.10. If it is zero, \(w'' = 0\) on the open pieces. By corollary 1.85 with \(w'\), \(w'\) is constant on every piece, and since \(w'\) is continuous, it is the same constant \(b\) on all pieces. The function \(w - b\,x\) has derivative zero on every piece, so it is constant on a piece, and since it is continuous, it is the same constant \(a\) everywhere. The variation \(w = a + b\,x\) is admissible, so by the assumption on the supports it is the zero function.

Source: The proof is not from a source. Bar: EP §4.3.1 (pp. 179-183) and EP (3.3.3), (3.3.4) (p. 124) for the total potential energy, beam: the same sources as corollary 5.74.

What did the proof show? Both principles stay valid, because the terms at the break points cancel thanks to continuity, and because a nonnegative continuous function with zero integral is zero everywhere on every piece. Continuity is essential in two places: the function \(u\) (or for the beam \(v\) and \(v'\)) and the force \(N\) (or \(V\) and \(M\)) must not jump. A jump of \(N\) would give an extra term at the break point, as in the example below lemma 6.13. A jump of \(v'\) would give a term equal to the moment \(M\) times the jump, which for \(M \neq 0\) would not vanish.

Let us test the principle on the stepped bar (section 6.1.3). As a trial field take the straight line \(\tilde u = c\,x\), which chapter 4 used as the first trial field. The function \(\tilde u\) has one piece here and \(u\) has two, but the difference \(\tilde u - u\) is piecewise continuously differentiable with the break point \(x = 5\) m. The best \(c\) from the minimum of \(\Pi(c\,x)\) gives the end displacement \(\tilde u(L) = 13{,}66\) µm instead of \(12{,}20\) µm. The energy is \(\Pi(\tilde u) = -89{,}81\) µJ, and that of the true field \(\Pi(u) = -106{,}92\) µJ. The difference is \(17{,}11\) µJ. The integral \(\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,(\tilde u' - u')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) is a sum over pieces, \(\int_0^5 \dots + \int_5^{10} \dots\), and gives the same number \(17{,}11\) µJ, as item 2 requires. Item 1 with \(\delta u = x\) gives on the left \(\int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x = 131{,}46\) N m and on the right \(\int_0^L q\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = 131{,}46\) N m, where \(q\) is the weight per unit length, \(\rho g A\) above and \(\rho g A/4\) below.

For the beam take a cantilever of length \(L = 1\) m with a vertical force of \(500\) N downward at the free end, as in chapter 5, but with a bending stiffness that is reduced at the middle: \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m² for \(x < 0{,}5\) m and half of that value for \(x > 0{,}5\) m (a step in the cross-section, which the model idealizes as a jump, as for the bar). The moment \(M = -500\ \text{N}\,(L - x)\) is continuous, so the curvature \(v'' = M/EI\) jumps at \(x = 0{,}5\) m from \(-0{,}011\,958\ \text{m}^{-1}\) to \(-0{,}023\,916\ \text{m}^{-1}\), and \(v'\) is continuous. The true end displacement is \(-8{,}968\) mm, the energy \(\Pi(v) = -2{,}242\) J. The trial parabola \(\tilde v = a\,x^2\) has the best \(a = -7{,}972 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), end displacement \(-7{,}972\) mm and \(\Pi(\tilde v) = -1{,}993\) J. The difference \(0{,}249\) J equals the integral \(\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EI\,(\tilde v'' - v'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), computed piece by piece, as item 4 requires.

6.2.3 The general setting

Everything we proved holds for functions that are continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable, and for the Riemann integral. The mathematics that treats these problems in general uses a larger class of functions. The space \(L^2\) (space of square integrable functions, prostor kvadratno integrabilnih funkcij) consists of the functions whose square has a finite integral (EP (6.2.6), (6.2.7), p. 274, BATHE PDF p. 253). The Sobolev space \(H^1\) (Sobolev space, Sobolevov prostor) consists of the functions whose square and whose derivative's square have a finite integral (EP (6.2.22), p. 279, BATHE PDF p. 254). For a bar with positive stiffness this is the class of functions with finite energy \(\tfrac12\int EA\,u'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). BATHE counts in it also the trial fields of the finite element method (BATHE, PDF p. 256, "Of course, \(V_{\mathrm{h}} \subset V\)"). Every piecewise continuously differentiable function also has finite energy, since its derivative is continuous and therefore bounded on every piece.

Why do mathematicians need it? In this chapter we proved the minimum energy for fields that we know how to write down, and for the true field we had in every case a formula that integration gave. A general theorem must show that a minimum of the energy exists at all. We measure the distance between two fields here by the energy of their difference, \(\int \tfrac12\,EA\,(\tilde u' - u')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), as in item 2 of corollary 6.14. A space is complete (poln) if every sequence of fields whose terms come ever closer to each other by this distance has a limit in the space. EP says that the space \(H_{\mathrm{A}}\) consisting of the fields with finite energy is complete with respect to this distance, that is a Hilbert space (EP pp. 287 and 281). The potential energy \(\Pi\), which assigns a number to a field, extends to the whole space and attains its minimum there at exactly one function. The proofs go beyond EP, which leaves them to the literature (EP p. 287). The space of continuously differentiable functions is not complete for the Sobolev norm, and its completion is the Sobolev space (EP p. 278). This means that the minimum may be attained only in a class larger than ours.

In this book we do not need this, because for bars and beams we obtain the true field by integration (chapters 4 and 5), so the existence of the minimum energy is already proved. The Sobolev space needs the Lebesgue integral, which the book does not have, so we only name it. For bodies in the plane and in space the existence of a solution does not follow from integration. Each time we state that the claim holds if a solution exists, and we leave existence to chapter 11.

6.3 Mathematics: inner product of functions

In section 4.6.8 we computed the hanging bar with the trial field \(c\,x\) (poskusno polje) with one free number \(c\). The best line gave the right displacement at the lower end and underestimated it in the middle of the bar. With one more free number we can do better. Take \(u = c_1\,x + c_2\,x^2\) with free numbers \(c_1\) and \(c_2\), which we call coefficients (koeficienta). The bar has length \(L = 10\) m and the same data as in chapter 4, \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N, \(q = 6{,}010\) N/m. Both fields \(x\) and \(x^2\) respect the fixing at \(x = 0\).

  1. The derivative of the field is \(u' = c_1 + 2 c_2\,x\). By the linearity of the integral and the fundamental theorem of calculus, the potential energy from corollary 4.93 (there is no force at the lower end) is
    \[\begin{aligned} \Pi(c_1, c_2) &= \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,(c_1 + 2 c_2 x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,(c_1 x + c_2 x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \tfrac12\,EA\Big(L\,c_1^2 + 2 L^2 c_1 c_2 + \tfrac43 L^3 c_2^2\Big) - q\Big(\tfrac12 L^2 c_1 + \tfrac13 L^3 c_2\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
  2. By section 4.6.6 both partial derivatives are zero at the lowest point. The derivative with respect to \(c_1\) and with respect to \(c_2\) gives two equations, linear in the unknowns \(c_1\) and \(c_2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} EA\,L\,c_1 + EA\,L^2\,c_2 &= \tfrac12\,q L^2 , \\ EA\,L^2\,c_1 + \tfrac43\,EA\,L^3\,c_2 &= \tfrac13\,q L^3 . \end{aligned} \tag{6.9}\]
  3. From the first equation \(c_1 = qL/(2EA) - L\,c_2\). We insert it into the second: \(\tfrac12\,qL^3 + \tfrac13\,EA\,L^3 c_2 = \tfrac13\,qL^3\), so \(c_2 = -q/(2EA) = -a\) and \(c_1 = qL/EA = 2aL\), where \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) as in section 3.1. The field is \(u = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), which is the true field of the bar.

The true field is a quadratic polynomial, so the fields \(c_1 x + c_2 x^2\) contain it and we obtain it exactly. Now we ask what kind of equations we have obtained. In the system (6.9) every coefficient is an integral of a product of derivatives of two trial functions, for example \(EA\,L^2 = \int_0^L EA \cdot 1 \cdot 2x\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the product of the derivatives of the functions \(x\) and \(x^2\). The coefficient \(EA\,L^2\) stands in both equations because the product of the derivatives of the same two functions does not depend on their order. With \(n\) trial functions we shall get \(n\) such equations with \(n \times n\) coefficients. When does the system have exactly one solution, and why is it hard to solve in some cases? The answer comes from ideas we know from vectors in space. In this section we carry them over to functions, then show that the coefficients of the system are scalar products of the trial functions, and from this we derive when the system has a single solution.

6.3.1 Functions as vectors

In section 1.5.3 we already saw that functions defined for all numbers between two numbers are vectors in the sense of definition 1.16, since we add them point by point (figure 1.25). The trial fields of the hanging bar are not all such functions. They must be continuous, piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11) and equal to zero at \(x = 0\), because the bar is fixed there. Do they form a vector space? For that we must check that the sum of two such functions and a multiple of such a function again belong to them.

Lemma 6.15 Fields of a bar form a vector space (polja palice so vektorski prostor)

Let \(L > 0\) and let \(X\) be the set of all functions \(w : [0, L] \to \mathbb{R}\) that are continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11). With addition point by point and multiplication by a number point by point, \(X\) is a vector space. The set \(W\) of those functions of \(X\) that are zero at the fixed ends of the bar is a vector space too. For a bar fixed at \(x = 0\) these are the test functions of the weak form (definition 6.2), the functions with \(w(0) = 0\).

Proof

We must show that the sum and the multiple stay in \(X\) and in \(W\) and that the rules of definition 1.16 hold.

  1. Let \(w_1, w_2 \in X\) with the partitions of definition 6.11. We take the common partition, which has the break points of both. Each of its pieces lies in a piece of the first and in a piece of the second partition, so \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) have on an open piece a derivative that equals a function continuous on the closed piece.
  2.
