Source: BATHE (4.89) to (4.91) (PDF p. 258, "the strain energy corresponding to the finite element solution is always smaller than or equal to"), COOK PDF p. 164 ("either exact or too stiff", the computed strain energy is a lower bound). For the bar point 1 is the computation of corollary 4.93, for the beam of corollary 5.74 and for the body of theorem 4.91, written here with the weak form. The proof in steps is not from the sources.

Point 1 of the proof does not use \(\psi_0 = 0\), so it holds also for a prescribed displacement of a support. Point 2 does not: for the bar fixed at both ends with the settlement \(d = 0{,}1\) mm (subsection 6.4.2), \(u\) is a field with the prescribed \(u(L) = d\), which is not a test function, and \(B(u, u) - \ell(u) = N(L)\,d = 123{,}89\ \text{N} \cdot 0{,}1\ \text{mm} = 12{,}39\) mJ, not zero (computed with SymPy).

The proof showed two things. The Ritz energy is above the true one by exactly the strain energy of the error that the trial family missed, and the work of the loads on the Ritz field is always too small because of the equality \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, u_{\mathrm{n}}) = \ell(u_{\mathrm{n}})\). A test on the hanging bar: the work of the weight on the true field is \(782{,}06\) µJ, on the cubic Ritz field \(763{,}73\) µJ, so 2,3 % less. The strain energy is \(381{,}87\) against \(391{,}03\) µJ. The difference of the energies, \(9{,}165\) µJ, is the strain energy of the error \(u - u_1\) (computed with SymPy), as the proof predicts. For zero essential conditions one more conclusion follows from point 2: if the family contains the true field, Ritz finds it, because \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) \le \Pi(u)\) (the smallest value in the family) and by point 1 at the same time \(\ge\), so equality holds and \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = u\). This is how we got the exact result for the cantilever with a force at the end with \(x^2, x^3\) and for the cantilever under its own weight with \(x^2, x^3, x^4\).

What does the theorem not say? It does not say that every displacement is too small. The work of the loads on the field is an average over the loaded part, while the displacement at one point is a single value. For the hanging bar the work of the weight is 2,3 % too small, while the displacement of the end is 4,2 % too large. It shows more strongly on the stepped bar of section 6.1.3, with the upper \(5\) m of diameter \(10\) mm and the lower \(5\) m of diameter \(5\) mm. The Ritz solution with the single trial function \(\psi = x\) is the best line of section 6.2.2, with the displacement of the end \(13{,}66\) µm instead of \(12{,}20\) µm, 12 % too high. By item 2 the work of the weight is \(-2\Pi\), so with the energies \(-89{,}81\) and \(-106{,}92\) µJ of the same section it is \(179{,}6\) µJ against the true \(213{,}8\) µJ, 16 % too small, as the theorem demands. Ritz therefore bounds the work of the loads, but not every displacement.

The rule holds for the displacement under a force if it is the only load. For one force \(F\) at a point \(P\), \(\ell(w) = F\,w(P)\), so \(\ell(u_{\mathrm{n}}) \le \ell(u)\) means \(F\,u_{\mathrm{n}}(P) \le F\,u(P)\): the displacement of the point \(P\) in the direction of the force is never too large. For the cantilever with a force at the end this is \(\tfrac34\) of the true value and with \(x^2, x^3\) exactly one. COOK (PDF p. 164) writes the same: under a single concentrated force the displacement at its point is certain to be underpredicted, or at best exact in a very simple problem, never overpredicted. COOK does not treat the cantilever there, the two numbers are ours. The common shortening "Ritz displacements are always too small" is wrong, as the hanging bar with its 4,2 % too high displacement of the end shows. The correct statement is: the displacement under the only force is too small or exact, the work of all the loads is too small or exact, and individual displacements can be on either side.

The last example shows how a family of fields can turn out to be too stiff. Take the hanging bar as a body in space, as in section 3.1.5, with a cross section of area \(A\) and a free lateral side. The upper face has a support that holds only the displacement in the direction of the axis, \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), and other supports prevent rigid movements (an idealization: a real support would also hold the lateral displacements at the edge of the face and give a stress concentration). The true field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with the lateral thinning, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (chapter 3), \(\nu = 0{,}3\). The trial field \(\vek u = c\,(2Lx - x^2)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) prevents the thinning, \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).

  1. The strains of the field are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2c\,(L - x)\), all the others are zero, because \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero and \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\).
  2. By Hooke's law (3.13), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Since of the strains only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is different from zero, \(\ten\sigma : \ten\varepsilon = (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\).
  3. For \(\psi = 2Lx - x^2\), \(K = A\,(\lambda + 2\mu) \int_0^L 4\,(L - x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac43\,A\,(\lambda + 2\mu)\,L^3\) and \(f = \rho g A \int_0^L \psi\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac23\,\rho g A\,L^3\).
  4. So \(c = \rho g/\big(2\,(\lambda + 2\mu)\big)\). The displacement of the end is \(c\,L^2 = \dfrac{E}{\lambda + 2\mu}\,\dfrac{\rho g L^2}{2E}\).

For steel \(\lambda + 2\mu = 263{,}85\) GPa (definition 3.10), the ratio \(E/(\lambda + 2\mu) = (1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)/(1 - \nu) = 0{,}7429\) and the displacement of the end \(14{,}50\) µm against \(19{,}52\) µm. The cause is the thinning (figure 6.15). The true field thins freely in the lateral direction, so for a uniaxial load \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The trial field does not allow the thinning and must have lateral stresses \(\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which the body does not have in uniaxial tension, so the material resists with \(\lambda + 2\mu = 263{,}85\) GPa instead of \(E = 196\) GPa, which is \(1{,}346\) times stronger. The solution is too stiff, the displacement of the end is \(0{,}743\) of the true one, and the work of the weight is smaller in the same ratio, as the theorem demands. A family of fields that prevents a deformation that the body needs under this load therefore gives a too stiff solution. The phenomenon is called locking (zaklepanje) and it will appear again in the finite elements of beams and of the continuum (chapters 12 and 15).

6.4.5 A sequence of ever richer families (zaporedje vse bogatejših družin)

We know that the Ritz solution for a given \(n\) is the best in its family. What happens when we increase \(n\), and when does the approximation approach the true solution? In chapter 4 we wrote that a richer family that contains a poorer one does not give a worse estimate. Now we prove this and add when the limit is the true one.

Let \(\mathcal V_1 \subset \mathcal V_2 \subset \dots\), where each family contains the previous one, with a common \(\psi_0\). Such are the families of polynomials \(x, x^2, \dots, x^n\), where each family adds one function, and the piecewise linear fields on meshes, where we get each mesh by halving the pieces of the previous one, because a line on a large piece is a line also on both halves (section 6.7).

Theorem 6.35 Convergence of Ritz solutions (konvergenca Ritzovih rešitev)

Within theorem 6.34, let \(\mathcal V_1 \subset \mathcal V_2 \subset \dots\) be a sequence of trial spaces with the same \(\psi_0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) the Ritz solution in \(\psi_0 + \mathcal V_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then \(\Pi(u_1) \ge \Pi(u_2) \ge \dots \ge \Pi(u)\) and \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}\) does not grow. If moreover for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exist \(N\) and a field \(v \in \psi_0 + \mathcal V_{\mathrm{N}}\) with \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}} < \varepsilon\) (completeness), then \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}} \to 0\) and \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) \to \Pi(u)\).

Proof

We must show that a larger family cannot give a higher energy, and then that under the condition of completeness the energy of the error falls below every bound.

  1. The field \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) is in \(\psi_0 + \mathcal V_{\mathrm{n}} \subset \psi_0 + \mathcal V_{\mathrm{n}+1}\). By definition (theorem 6.33, point 3) the field \(u_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) has the smallest energy in the larger family, so \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}+1}) \le \Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}})\).
  2. By theorem 6.34, point 1, \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) \ge \Pi(u)\) and \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = 2\,\big(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) - \Pi(u)\big)\). A decreasing energy therefore means a decreasing energy norm of the error, which is the first claim.
  3. For completeness let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(N\), \(v\) as in the theorem. For \(n \ge N\), \(v \in \psi_0 + \mathcal V_{\mathrm{N}} \subset \psi_0 + \mathcal V_{\mathrm{n}}\), so \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) \le \Pi(v)\).
  4. By point 2 and step 3, \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = 2\,\big(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) - \Pi(u)\big) \le 2\,\big(\Pi(v) - \Pi(u)\big) = \|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 < \varepsilon^2\), where we got the last equality from theorem 6.34, point 1, for the field \(v\) (it is admissible, but not necessarily the Ritz one).
  5. For every \(\varepsilon\) there exists \(N\) such that for \(n \ge N\), \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}} < \varepsilon\), so \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}} \to 0\) (definition 1.38). From \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) - \Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\) it follows that \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{n}}) \to \Pi(u)\).

Source: COOK §4.9 (PDF p. 176, "monotonic convergence of structural strain energy"), EP p. 299, point 4 (convergence when the requirements are met, without proof), BATHE PDF p. 258 (a larger space, a greater accuracy). The proof in steps is not from the sources. EP has no explicit statement of monotonicity for nested families.

The theorem showed that the energy cannot increase when the family is enriched, and that the error falls below every bound if the family allows it. Step 3 does not require \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) to be close to the field \(v\), only that it is not worse than it in energy.

Let us test it on the sequences. For the hanging bar take piecewise linear fields on \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16\) equal pieces: for \(n = 1\) this is the line \(c\,x\) of chapter 4. The energies are \(-293{,}27\), \(-366{,}59\), \(-384{,}92\), \(-389{,}50\) and \(-390{,}65\) µJ against \(-391{,}03\) µJ (figure 6.16), the differences are \(97{,}76/n^2\) µJ. For the cantilever under its own weight with the polynomials \(x^2\), \(x^3\), \(x^4\) the energies are \(-2489{,}4\), \(-4356{,}4\) and \(-4480{,}9\) µJ, from the third term on exactly the true one, because the true deflection lies in the family. In both sequences each energy is below the previous one and above the true one, as the theorem demands.

Is completeness satisfied? For piecewise linear fields we prove it in section 6.5 (theorem 6.41). For polynomials it is given by Weierstrass's theorem: every continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated by a polynomial as closely as we wish at all points (LEBL2, theorem 11.7.1, PDF p. 179). For a bar with constant \(EA\) whose true solution has a continuous derivative \(u'\) and \(\psi_0 = 0\), we take a polynomial \(p\) with \(|u' - p| < \delta\) everywhere and \(v(x) = \int_0^x p\,\mathrm{d}t\), which is a combination of the functions \(x, x^2, \dots, x^n\) for \(n\) large enough. Then \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = \int_0^L EA\,(u' - p)^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le EA\,L\,\delta^2\), as small as we wish. For a beam whose true deflection has a continuous second derivative we do the same with the second derivative. No result of the book rests on this theorem, and the completeness of piecewise linear fields we prove ourselves.

The theorem needs nested families. The uniform meshes with two and three pieces are not one inside the other, because the nodes at \(10/3\) and \(20/3\) m do not coincide with the node at \(5\) m. The theorem then says nothing about the order of their solutions. For our bar the energy of the error still falls, \(24{,}44\) µJ at \(n = 2\) and \(10{,}86\) µJ at \(n = 3\). For every uniform \(n\) the energy of the error is \(EA\,a^2 L^3/(6n^2)\), which we checked with SymPy for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16\).

The Ritz method is thus explained: as many functions as we like, one solution, an energy above the true one and decreasing as the family is enriched. What remains is the question of how fast and in which quantities the error falls, and when the displacement at a point is exact in spite of the error elsewhere. This will be section 6.5.

6.5 How good is the approximation

Chapter 4 tried a line and a parabola on the hanging bar and noted two findings for the line. The error of the best line has the smallest strain energy, 97,76 µJ, and the displacement of the lower end is exactly right (section 4.6.8). The Ritz method (definition 6.32) now allows as many parameters as we like. We ask three questions. Does the Ritz method always choose the field whose error has the smallest energy? When is the displacement of a chosen point exact, and not only approximate? How fast does the error fall as we improve the trial family? Each question is followed by a theorem, which we test on the hanging bar and on the bar with a step.

The notation is that of section 6.4. For a bar the bilinear form \(B(u, w)\) (definition 6.4) is \(\int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\), the linear form \(\ell(w)\) is the work of the given loads on the field \(w\), \(u\) is the solution of the weak form (definition 6.6), \(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the trial space (poskusni prostor), that is all sums \(c_1\psi_1 + \dots + c_{\mathrm{n}}\psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) of trial functions that satisfy the homogeneous essential conditions, \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the Ritz solution in \(\psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(e_{\mathrm{n}} = u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\) is its error. The energy of a field \(w\) is \(U(w) = \tfrac12 B(w, w)\) and its energy norm is \(\|w\|_{\mathrm{E}} = \sqrt{B(w, w)}\) (definition 6.18). The energy of the error \(U(e_{\mathrm{n}})\) is therefore \(\tfrac12\|e_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\).

6.5.1 The error is orthogonal to the trial fields

For the best line the error \(a\,(Lx - x^2)\) was orthogonal to the trial field \(x\) in the energy inner product, \(B(e_1, x) = \int_0^L EA\,a\,(L - 2x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) (section 6.3.2). Does this hold only for a line? The idea of the proof is simple. The Ritz solution is the lowest point of the energy on the trial family. If we move it in the direction of one of the trial functions, the energy must not decrease, and to first order it changes by \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) - \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\). This is exactly the \(i\)-th Ritz equation. From it and from the weak form for the true field it follows that the error is orthogonal to all trial functions.

Lemma 6.36 Galerkin orthogonality (Galerkinova ortogonalnost)

Let \(B\) and \(\ell\) be the bilinear and the linear form of a bar, a beam or a body. Let \(u\) be the solution of the weak form, \(B(u, w) = \ell(w)\) for every test function \(w\), and let \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = \psi_0 + c_1\psi_1 + \dots + c_{\mathrm{n}}\psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the Ritz solution with the trial functions of definition 6.32. Then

\[B(u - u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) = 0 \quad \text{for every } w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}} . \tag{6.20}\]
Proof

We must show that at every trial field the error does the same work as the true field, so that the difference is zero.

  1. Every \(w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) is a linear combination of the test functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and is therefore a test function, because these form a vector space \(W\) (definition 6.6). The weak form says \(B(u, w) = \ell(w)\).
  2. The Ritz equations are \(K c = f\) with \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) and \(f_{\mathrm{i}} = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}) - B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) (definition 6.32). Written row by row they say \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\,c_{\mathrm{j}} = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}) - B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\). By linearity of \(B\) in the first argument, \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\).
  3. Let \(w = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} d_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\). We multiply the equation of step 2 by \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\) and sum over \(i\). By linearity of \(B\) in the second argument and of \(\ell\), \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) = \ell(w)\).
  4. We subtract the equation of step 3 from the equation of step 1. By linearity of \(B\) in the first argument, \(B(u, w) - B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) = B(u - u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) = \ell(w) - \ell(w) = 0\).

Source: BATHE (4.86) to (4.88), property 1 (PDF p. 258), where the orthogonality (4.86) in \(a(\cdot, \cdot)\) is proved by subtracting the equations of the principle of virtual work. The proof in steps is ours.

The proof showed that the orthogonality of the error says the same as the Ritz equations, only written differently. The name comes from the method of the next section, which has the same equations and therefore the same orthogonality also where there is no energy.

We check it on the hanging bar with the cubic trial field \(\psi = 3L^2 x - x^3\) from section 6.4.2. The Ritz solution is \(u_1 = c\,\psi\) with \(c = \tfrac{25}{96}\,q/(EA\,L)\), where \(q/(EA) = 2a\) and \(a = \rho g/(2E)\) (chapter 4). Hence \(c = \tfrac{25}{48}\,a/L\). The derivatives are \(u' = 2a\,(L - x)\) and \(u_1' = c\,\psi' = \tfrac{25}{16}\,(a/L)\,(L^2 - x^2)\), and the error has the derivative

\[e_1' = a\,(L - x)\Big(2 - \frac{25\,(L + x)}{16\,L}\Big) = \frac{a\,(L - x)(7L - 25x)}{16\,L} .\]

Since \(\psi' = 3\,(L - x)(L + x)\),

\[B(e_1, \psi) = \frac{3\,EA\,a}{16\,L} \int_0^L (L - x)^2 (L + x)(7L - 25x)\,\mathrm{d}x .\]

For \(L = 1\) the product under the integral is \((1 - x)^2(1 + x)(7 - 25x) = 7 - 32x + 18x^2 + 32x^3 - 25x^4\) and the integral is \(7 - 16 + 6 + 8 - 5 = 0\). The orthogonality holds here too (checked with SymPy). The Pythagorean theorem for energies (lemma 6.21) applied to \(e_1 \perp u_1\) gives \(U(u) = U(u_1) + U(e_1)\), that is \(381{,}87 + 9{,}165 = 391{,}03\) µJ. The same as for the line: \(293{,}27 + 97{,}76 = 391{,}03\) µJ.

By theorem 6.34 the energy of the error \(U(e_1) = 9{,}165\) µJ is also the difference of the energies \(\Pi(u_1) - \Pi(u)\) (section 6.4.4). What remains is the question whether this is the smallest error in the family.

Theorem 6.37 Best approximation in the energy norm (najboljši približek v energijski normi)

Let \(B\) be a symmetric bilinear form that is positive on the test functions, that is \(B(w, w) > 0\) for every test function \(w \ne 0\) (lemma 6.7). Let \(u\) and \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) be as in lemma 6.36. Then for every \(v \in \psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\)

\[\|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}} \le \|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}} , \tag{6.21}\]

with equality only for \(v = u_{\mathrm{n}}\). More precisely, \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = \|u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 + \|u_{\mathrm{n}} - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\).

Proof

We must show that the error of an arbitrary field of the family splits into the error of the Ritz solution and a part inside the family, and that the two are orthogonal.

  1. Let \(e = u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(d = u_{\mathrm{n}} - v\). The fields \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(v\) have the same \(\psi_0\), which cancels in the difference, so \(d\) is a sum of functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\), that is \(d \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. We have \(u - v = e + d\). By bilinearity and symmetry of \(B\), \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = B(e + d, e + d) = B(e, e) + 2B(e, d) + B(d, d)\).
  3. By lemma 6.36, \(B(e, d) = 0\), because \(d \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\). Hence \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = \|e\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 + \|d\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\).
  4. Since \(\|d\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = B(d, d) \ge 0\), we have \(\|e\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 \le \|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\), and the square root of both sides gives equation (6.21).
  5. If \(\|e\|_{\mathrm{E}} = \|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}\), then by step 3 \(\|d\|_{\mathrm{E}} = 0\), so \(d = 0\) by the positivity of the form \(B\) and \(v = u_{\mathrm{n}}\).

Source: BATHE (4.91)-(4.94), property 3 (PDF p. 258-259): "the strain energy corresponding to \(u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the minimum". The proof in steps is ours.

The proof showed that among all fields of the family the Ritz method chooses the one whose error has the smallest energy, and that every other field is worse by exactly the energy of its difference from the Ritz field (figure 6.17). For the line we only observed this (section 4.6.8).

We test it on the cubic family \(v = c\,\psi\) with \(c\) in units of \(q/(EA\,L)\). By the theorem \(U(u - v) = U(e_1) + U(u_1 - v)\) must hold, as the table shows.

\(c\) \(U(u - v)\) (µJ) \(U(u_1 - v)\) (µJ) end (µm)
\(25/96\) (Ritz) 9,165 0 20,33
\(1/4\) (least squares, next section) 9,776 0,611 19,52
\(1/3\) (collocation, next section) 39,10 29,94 26,03
\(1/2\) 332,4 323,2 39,04

In every row \(9{,}165 + U(u_1 - v) = U(u - v)\) (SymPy), for example \(9{,}165 + 0{,}611 = 9{,}776\) µJ. The energy of the difference is quadratic in \(c\), \(U(u_1 - v) = 5631\,(c - 25/96)^2\) µJ, a parabola with its lowest point at the Ritz value. The end displacement is not so orderly: least squares give the exact displacement 19,52 µm and a larger energy of the error than Ritz. The best in energy therefore does not mean the best at every point. In the next section we shall see when the displacement at a point is nevertheless exact.

6.5.2 When the displacement at a point is exact

Chapter 4 found for the best line that the displacement of the lower end is exact, and wrote that this is no coincidence. The reason given was that the line is the average of the true strain. Now we can pose the general question: for which points and which families is the Ritz displacement exact? Theorem 6.37 measures the error by the energy over the whole bar and says nothing about a single point. The answer comes from the work of a force. The displacement of a point \(P\) in the direction of a force is the work of a unit force at \(P\) on that displacement. The same work can be expressed by the strain energy of the field that the unit force causes.

Take a bar with axial stiffness \(EA\), positive and piecewise continuous (as for the bar with a step), fixed at \(x = 0\). Let \(P\) be the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) the displacement of this bar when only a unit force \(1\) N acts on it at \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) in the direction of the \(x\) axis. The axial force between the fixing and the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) is \(1\) N (tension), since the fixing must hold this force, and beyond \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) it is zero, because there are no loads. Therefore

\[\begin{aligned} G_{\mathrm{P}}(x) &= \int_0^{\min(x,\, x_{\mathrm{P}})} \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{EA(t)} , \\ G_{\mathrm{P}}' &= \frac{1}{EA} \ \text{ for } x < x_{\mathrm{P}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{P}}' = 0 \ \text{ for } x > x_{\mathrm{P}} . \end{aligned} \tag{6.22}\]

The field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) increases up to the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and is constant beyond it (figure 6.18). It is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11), it has a kink at \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\), and \(G_{\mathrm{P}}(0) = 0\).

Theorem 6.38 Exactness of the displacement at a point (točnost pomika v točki)

Let the bar be fixed at \(x = 0\), with axial stiffness \(EA > 0\), piecewise continuous, and with arbitrary given loads. Let \(u\) be the solution of the weak form and \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) the Ritz solution in \(\psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) with the essential condition \(u(0) = 0\) (or \(u(0)\) given, the same for both). Let \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) be the field of the unit force at the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) from equation (6.22). If \(G_{\mathrm{P}} \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\), then

\[u_{\mathrm{n}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}) = u(x_{\mathrm{P}}) .\]
Proof

We must show that the error at the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) is the work of a unit force on the error, and that this work is zero by the orthogonality of the error to the trial fields.

  1. For every admissible \(w\) with \(w(0) = 0\), \(B(G_{\mathrm{P}}, w) = \int_0^L EA\,G_{\mathrm{P}}'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\). By equation (6.22), \(EA\,G_{\mathrm{P}}' = 1\) on \((0, x_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(0\) on \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, L)\), so \(B(G_{\mathrm{P}}, w) = \int_0^{x_{\mathrm{P}}} w'\,\mathrm{d}x = w(x_{\mathrm{P}}) - w(0) = w(x_{\mathrm{P}})\) by lemma 6.12.
  2. The error \(e = u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\) is a test function \(w\), since \(u\) and \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) are piecewise continuously differentiable and have the same value at \(x = 0\), so \(e(0) = 0\). Step 1 with \(w = e\) gives \(e(x_{\mathrm{P}}) = B(G_{\mathrm{P}}, e)\).
  3. The form \(B\) is symmetric, \(B(G_{\mathrm{P}}, e) = B(e, G_{\mathrm{P}})\), because the integrand \(EA\,G_{\mathrm{P}}'\,e'\) is symmetric in the two fields (definition 6.4).
  4. Since \(G_{\mathrm{P}} \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\), by lemma 6.36 \(B(e, G_{\mathrm{P}}) = 0\).
  5. From steps 2 to 4, \(e(x_{\mathrm{P}}) = 0\), so \(u_{\mathrm{n}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}) = u(x_{\mathrm{P}})\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The theorem explains observations that sources state without a reason: exact nodal values for two-node bars (ONATE1, PDF p. 363, "the displacement solution for 2-noded bar elements is exact at the nodes").

The proof showed that the error at a point is the work of a unit force on the error (the principle of virtual displacements for the field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) with the virtual displacement \(e\)) and that the orthogonality cancels this work when \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) is in the family. The exchange of the roles of the two fields in step 3 is for a body stated by Betti's theorem (theorem 4.137), and for a bar the symmetry of the form \(B\) gives it here already. We test the theorem on four examples.

The line on the hanging bar. The family \(\{c\,x\}\) contains \(G_{\mathrm{L}} = x/EA\), the field of the unit force at the lower end (\(x_{\mathrm{P}} = L\), \(\min(x, L) = x\) and \(EA\) is constant). Hence \(u_1(L) = u(L) = 19{,}52\) µm. This explains the phenomenon from chapter 4. At the middle of the bar (\(x_{\mathrm{P}} = L/2\)), however, the field \(G_{\mathrm{L}/2} = \min(x, L/2)/EA\) is not a line, since it has a kink, and indeed the line gives 9,760 µm instead of 14,64 µm.

The cubic trial field. For \(\psi = 3L^2 x - x^3\) the field \(G_{\mathrm{L}} = x/EA\) is not in the family \(\{c\,\psi\}\), and the theorem is silent. The end displacement is 20,33 µm instead of 19,52 µm. Step 2 of the proof still holds. The error of the end displacement is \(e(L) = -0{,}813\) µm and \(B(G_{\mathrm{L}}, e_1)\) is exactly this much (SymPy). This value is not zero because step 4 fails: \(G_{\mathrm{L}} \notin \mathcal{V}_1\), so \(B(e_1, G_{\mathrm{L}}) \ne 0\).

The bar with a step. The upper 5 m of the bar have a diameter of 10 mm, the lower 5 m a diameter of 5 mm, so \(EA\) drops to a quarter (section 6.1.3). The exact displacements are \(u(5) = 7{,}320\) µm and \(u(10) = 12{,}20\) µm. The field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) has the slope \(1/EA\), which increases fourfold at the step. Trial fields that are continuous and a line on each of two elements (hat functions, section 6.3.3) have exactly such a kink when the node is at the step. Two elements with a node at \(x = 5\) m contain \(G_5\) and \(G_{10}\), so both nodal values are exact (SymPy: 7,320 and 12,20 µm). With a single element over the whole bar \(G_{10}\) is not in the family and the end displacement is 13,66 µm, 12 % too much (section 6.2.2). The node must therefore be where \(EA\) changes. The same reason holds for every node: where \(EA\) is constant on each element, \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) for a node \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) is a line on each element, so it is in the family. For the hanging bar with \(n\) elements the nodal values are therefore exact for every \(n\) (SymPy for \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16\)), for two elements 14,64 and 19,52 µm.

The cantilever under its own weight. The theorem holds also for a beam with a force at the free end, with the same four steps. Let the cantilever of length \(L\) be clamped at \(x = 0\) and let a unit force act upward at the free end. The field \(G(x) = x^2\,(3L - x)/(6EI)\) has \(EI\,G'' = L - x\) and \(G(0) = G'(0) = 0\). For every admissible \(w\) with \(w(0) = w'(0) = 0\), integration by parts gives \(B(G, w) = \int_0^L (L - x)\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[(L - x)\,w'\big]_0^L + \int_0^L w'\,\mathrm{d}x = w(L)\), which is step 1. For \(L = 1\) m and \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\ \text{N m}^2\), \(G = (3x^2 - x^3)/125\,440\) and it lies in the family \(\{x^2, x^3\}\), but not in the family \(\{x^2\}\). Therefore the end displacement with two terms is exact, \(-0{,}3660\) mm, and with one term it is \(-0{,}2440\) mm, because the error is \(e(L) = B(G, e) = -0{,}1220\) mm. The clamping moment with two terms is not exact, however: it is \(-25{,}51\) N m instead of \(-30{,}61\) N m (17 % too little). The theorem is silent about this, because the moment is the second derivative of the field, not its value at a point.

The theorem has limits. First, the field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) belongs to one point. For two elements on the hanging bar the nodal values are exact, but at the middle of an element the error is \(1{,}220\) µm, because the field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) for this point has a kink in the middle of an element and is not in the family. This error is \(a\,h^2/4\) with \(h = 5\) m, and in section 6.5.4 we shall see how it falls with \(h\). Second, the theorem says nothing about quantities that are not the value of a displacement at a point, for example the moment or the stress. Third, in a plane or spatial body the displacement under a point force is infinite (COOK, PDF p. 361: "Infinite displacement and infinite stress where P acts on a 2D or 3D solid"). The field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) has no finite energy there and cannot be in a family of fields with finite energy, so the theorem is not usable for a point force. Exactness at a point is a property of the one-dimensional model.

6.5.3 Cea's lemma for a bar

Theorem 6.37 measures the error in the energy norm, which contains the stiffness \(EA\). Often we are interested in the strain itself, that is the derivative \(u'\) and its error \(u' - u_{\mathrm{n}}'\), which is not weighted by \(EA\). Is the Ritz solution close to the best field of the family here too? For constant stiffness the answer is yes, since the energy norm is then \(\sqrt{EA}\) times the norm of the derivative. For the bar with a step the stiffness changes and the estimate needs bounds. We denote by \(\|f\| = \sqrt{\int_0^L f^2\,\mathrm{d}x}\) the norm of the inner product \((f, g) = \int_0^L f\,g\,\mathrm{d}x\) (definition 6.16).

Theorem 6.39 Cea's lemma for a bar (Ceajeva lema za palico)

Let the bar be fixed at \(x = 0\), \(EA\) piecewise continuous and \(m \le EA(x) \le M\) with \(m > 0\). Let \(u\) be the solution of the weak form and \(u_{\mathrm{n}} \in \psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) a field with \(B(u - u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) = 0\) for every \(w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\), for example the Ritz solution (lemma 6.36). Then for every \(v \in \psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\)

\[\|u' - u_{\mathrm{n}}'\| \le \frac{M}{m}\,\|u' - v'\| . \tag{6.23}\]

Since \(B\) is symmetric, even

\[\|u' - u_{\mathrm{n}}'\| \le \sqrt{\frac{M}{m}}\,\|u' - v'\| . \tag{6.24}\]
Proof

We must show that the energy of the error bounds the norm of the derivative of the error from below with \(m\), and that, thanks to the orthogonality, the energy of the error does not exceed the part of the error of an arbitrary field, with \(M\), from above.

  1. Let \(e = u - u_{\mathrm{n}}\). The field \(e\) is a test function, \(e(0) = 0\). We split \(e = (u - v) + (v - u_{\mathrm{n}})\), where \(v - u_{\mathrm{n}} \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\). By lemma 6.36, \(B(e, v - u_{\mathrm{n}}) = 0\), so \(B(e, e) = B(e, u - v)\).
  2. Since \(EA \ge m\) and \(e'^2 \ge 0\), by nonnegativity and linearity of the integral of piecewise continuous functions (lemma 6.10, points 2 and 3, for the difference \((EA - m)\,e'^2 \ge 0\)), \(B(e, e) = \int_0^L EA\,e'^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge m\,\|e'\|^2\).
  3. At every point \(EA\,e'\,(u - v)' \le M\,|e'|\,|(u - v)'|\), so by the same lemma, applied to the difference \(M\,|e'|\,|(u - v)'| - EA\,e'\,(u - v)' \ge 0\), \(B(e, u - v) \le M \int_0^L |e'|\,|(u - v)'|\,\mathrm{d}x = M\,(|e'|, |(u - v)'|)\). By lemma 6.19 this is at most \(M\,\|e'\|\,\|(u - v)'\|\). The lemma applies here because its proof uses only linearity in both arguments, symmetry and \((f, f) \ge 0\), which \((f, g) = \int_0^L f\,g\,\mathrm{d}x\) has for piecewise continuous functions (lemma 6.10).
  4. From steps 1 to 3, \(m\,\|e'\|^2 \le M\,\|e'\|\,\|(u - v)'\|\). If \(\|e'\| = 0\) the claim holds, otherwise we divide by \(m\,\|e'\|\) and obtain equation (6.23).
  5. For the symmetric case we take from step 2 the lower bound \(m\,\|e'\|^2 \le \|e\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\). As in steps 1 to 3 of the proof of theorem 6.37 (they use only orthogonality and symmetry, not the Ritz definition), \(u_{\mathrm{n}} - v \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = \|e\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 + \|u_{\mathrm{n}} - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 \ge \|e\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\). By the upper bound \(EA \le M\), \(\|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 \le M\,\|(u - v)'\|^2\). The chain of inequalities \(m\,\|e'\|^2 \le M\,\|(u - v)'\|^2\) gives, after division by \(m\) and the square root, equation (6.24).

Source: BATHE (4.95) (PDF p. 259): "This result is referred to as Cea's lemma", the constant is independent of \(h\) and dependent on the material properties. The proof in steps for a bar is ours.

The proof showed that the error of the Ritz method is at most a fixed number times the error of the best field of the family, and that this number depends only on the ratio of the extreme stiffnesses, not on the mesh. The first estimate (6.23) does not use symmetry, so it holds also for methods without energy, which we shall meet in the next section. For the second estimate symmetry saves a square root. BATHE (PDF p. 259, footnote 13) warns that for a body the constant grows when the bulk modulus is very large, and the estimate loses its meaning. This is another sign of locking (section 6.4.4), which chapters 12 and 15 treat.

We test it on the bar with a step, where \(M/m = 4\), so the constant of (6.23) is \(4\) and the constant of (6.24) is \(2\). The trial family is one element over the whole bar, \(\{c\,x\}\). The Ritz equation with the test function \(x\) gives \(c\int_0^L EA\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L EA\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x\), so \(c\) is the average of the true strain \(u'\) weighted by the stiffness: the upper part has four times the weight. The true field has the average derivative \(u(10)/10 = 1{,}220\) µm/m, the Ritz \(c = 1{,}366\) µm/m, 12 % more, which equals the ratio of the end displacements 13,66 and 12,20 µm. The best line in the norm of the derivative is the one with the plain average \(1{,}220\) µm/m. The ratio of norms is \(\|u' - c\|/\|u' - v'\| = 1{,}028\) (SymPy), far below the bounds 2 and 4 (figure 6.19). The bound holds for every load and every bar with the same \(M/m\), so it is loose here. For constant stiffness (\(M/m = 1\), the hanging bar) the constant is 1 and the Ritz solution is the best also in the norm of the derivative, which is theorem 6.37.

6.5.4 Error of piecewise linear interpolation

Cea's lemma and the theorem on the best approximation lead the error of the Ritz method back to the error of the best field of the family. We can estimate this if we can name some field of the family. For a family of fields that are a line on each element, such a field is the interpolant. Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be an element of length \(h = x_{\mathrm{b}} - x_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(u\) a field on it. The interpolant \(Iu\) is the line through the points \((x_{\mathrm{a}}, u(x_{\mathrm{a}}))\) and \((x_{\mathrm{b}}, u(x_{\mathrm{b}}))\) (figure 6.20). How much do \(u\) and \(u'\) differ from \(Iu\) and \((Iu)'\)? The answer must point to \(u''\): if \(u\) is a line the error is zero, and the larger the curvature, the larger the error.

Lemma 6.40 Error of piecewise linear interpolation (napaka odsekoma linearne interpolacije)

Let \(u\) have a continuous second derivative on \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) (one-sided at the end points), \(h = x_{\mathrm{b}} - x_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\mu = \max |u''|\) on this interval and \(Iu\) the line through the points \((x_{\mathrm{a}}, u(x_{\mathrm{a}}))\) and \((x_{\mathrm{b}}, u(x_{\mathrm{b}}))\). Then for every \(x \in [x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\)

  1. \(|u'(x) - (Iu)'| \le h\,\mu\),
  2. \(|u(x) - Iu(x)| \le \tfrac18\,h^2\,\mu\).
Proof

We must show that the derivative of the error changes by at most \(h\,\mu\) and that the error itself behaves like a parabola with zeros at the end points.

  1. The slope of the line \(Iu\) is \(k = (u(x_{\mathrm{b}}) - u(x_{\mathrm{a}}))/h\). The field \(u\) is continuous on \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) and differentiable, so by the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) there is \(\xi \in (x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}})\) with \(u'(\xi) = k\).
  2. The derivative \(u'\) is differentiable with derivative \(u''\), continuous on \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\), so by the same theorem for \(u'\) between \(\xi\) and \(x\) there is \(\eta\) with \(u'(x) - u'(\xi) = u''(\eta)\,(x - \xi)\). Since \(|x - \xi| \le h\) and \(|u''(\eta)| \le \mu\), \(|u'(x) - (Iu)'| = |u'(x) - u'(\xi)| \le h\,\mu\). This is point 1.
  3. For point 2 let \(x \in (x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}})\) (at the end points the error is zero). Let \(K = (u(x) - Iu(x))/((x - x_{\mathrm{a}})(x - x_{\mathrm{b}}))\) and \(g(t) = u(t) - Iu(t) - K\,(t - x_{\mathrm{a}})(t - x_{\mathrm{b}})\). The field \(g\) is continuous, twice differentiable and has zeros at \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(x\) and \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\).
  4. By Rolle's theorem (theorem 1.83), \(g'\) has a zero in \((x_{\mathrm{a}}, x)\) and a zero in \((x, x_{\mathrm{b}})\). By the same theorem for \(g'\) between these zeros there is \(\zeta \in (x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}})\) with \(g''(\zeta) = 0\).
  5. Since \(Iu\) is a line, \((Iu)'' = 0\), so \(g'' = u'' - 2K\) and \(K = u''(\zeta)/2\).
  6. Hence \(u(x) - Iu(x) = \tfrac12\,u''(\zeta)\,(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})(x - x_{\mathrm{b}})\). With \(s = x - (x_{\mathrm{a}} + x_{\mathrm{b}})/2\), \(|(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})(x - x_{\mathrm{b}})| = h^2/4 - s^2 \le h^2/4\), so \(|u(x) - Iu(x)| \le \tfrac12\,\mu\,h^2/4 = \tfrac18\,h^2\,\mu\). This is point 2.

Source: KREYSZIG §19.3, (5) (PDF p. 837), theorem 1 and example 3 (PDF p. 838) for the error of interpolation with a polynomial. The proof in steps is ours.

The proof showed that the error of the derivative follows from two uses of the mean value theorem and the error of the field from two uses of Rolle's theorem. A test on the hanging bar: \(u'' = -2a\) is constant, so \(\mu = 2a\), and point 2 gives \(\tfrac18\,h^2 \cdot 2a = a h^2/4\). The actual error is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 2a\,(x - x_{\mathrm{a}})(x_{\mathrm{b}} - x)\), largest at the middle of the element, \(a h^2/4\), so equality holds. For \(h = 5\) m, \(a h^2/4 = 1{,}220\) µm, and for \(h = 10\) m, \(4{,}880\) µm (SymPy). Point 1, however, is twice too large for the same field. The actual \(u' - (Iu)' = u''\,(x - x_{\text{middle}})\) reaches \(a h\) at the end points, and the estimate is \(2 a h\).

Now we can estimate the error of the Ritz method with hat functions. Let the bar be fixed at \(x = 0\) and let \(EA \le M\). We divide it by the nodes \(0 = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{n}} = L\) into the elements \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), the longest element having length \(h\). The trial space \(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{h}}\) consists of continuous fields that are a line on each element and have the value zero at \(x = 0\) (hat functions, section 6.3.3). We denote the Ritz solution in it by \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\).

Theorem 6.41 Convergence of piecewise linear fields (konvergenca odsekoma linearnih polj)

Let \(u\) be the solution of the weak form of a bar fixed at \(x = 0\), with piecewise continuous \(EA \le M\), and let \(u\) have a continuous second derivative on each element (the nodes are at the jumps of \(EA\)). Let \(\mu\) be the largest \(|u''|\) over all elements. Then

\[\|u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 \le M\,L\,h^2\,\mu^2 , \qquad \|u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\|_{\mathrm{E}} \le \sqrt{M L}\,h\,\mu , \tag{6.25}\]
\[0 \le \Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u) \le \tfrac12\,M\,L\,h^2\,\mu^2 . \tag{6.26}\]
Proof

We must show that the family contains a field whose error is estimated by the interpolation lemma, and that the Ritz error is at most that.

  1. Let \(v = Iu\) be the field that is on each element the interpolant of \(u\). It is continuous, because at a node it equals \(u(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) from both sides, it is a line on each element and \(v(0) = u(0) = 0\). So \(v \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{h}}\).
  2. By theorem 6.37, \(\|u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 \le \|u - v\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2 = \int_0^L EA\,((u - v)')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. On each element, by point 1 of lemma 6.40, \(|(u - v)'| \le h\,\mu\), since the length of the element is at most \(h\).
  4. Hence, because of \(EA \le M\) and nonnegativity of the integral (lemma 6.10, points 2 and 3, for the nonnegative difference \((M - EA)\,((u - v)')^2\)), \(\int_0^L EA\,((u - v)')^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le M\,h^2\,\mu^2\,L\). With step 2 this is the first inequality in equation (6.25), and the square root gives the second.
  5. By theorem 6.34, \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,\|u - u_{\mathrm{h}}\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\). This is not negative, and by step 4 it is not larger than \(\tfrac12\,M L\,h^2\,\mu^2\).

Source: BATHE §4.3.5, rate of convergence (PDF p. 261), where the rate is related to the order of the polynomials. The proof in steps is ours.

The proof showed that the error in energy falls as \(h^2\) and in the energy norm as \(h\), because the estimate of the derivative of the error grows as \(h\). At the same time this is the completeness of hat functions that theorem 6.35 needs: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is a mesh with \(\sqrt{M L}\,h\,\mu < \varepsilon\), so a field in the family with an error below \(\varepsilon\).

A test on the hanging bar (\(M = EA\), \(\mu = 2a\)) with uniform meshes \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16\) (table). The energy of the error is exactly \(97{,}76/n^2\) µJ, and the estimate (6.26) is \(1173/n^2\) µJ, for every \(n\) exactly 12 times more (SymPy).

\(n\) \(h\) (m) \(\Pi(u_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(u)\) (µJ) estimate (µJ) largest displacement error \(a h^2/4\) (µm)
1 10 97,76 1173 4,880
2 5 24,44 293,3 1,220
4 2,5 6,110 73,32 0,3050
8 1,25 1,527 18,33 0,07625
16 0,625 0,3819 4,582 0,01906

When we halve \(h\), the energy of the error is divided by 4 (figure 6.21). The reason is \(h^2\). The Ritz solution is here just the interpolant, \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = Iu\): the field \(G_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{i}}\) of the unit force at a node is continuous and a line on each element (the stiffness is constant), so it lies in \(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{h}}\), and the nodal values of \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) are therefore exact by theorem 6.38, while the line on an element is determined by its end points. For quadratic \(u\), \(u' - u_{\mathrm{h}}' = u''\,(x - x_{\text{middle}})\), the energy of the error on one element is therefore \(\tfrac12\,EA\,u''^2\,h^3/12\) and over \(n = L/h\) elements \(EA\,u''^2\,L\,h^2/24\). For \(u'' = -2a\) this is \(\tfrac16\,EA\,a^2 L\,h^2\), which for \(h = L/n\) gives \(97{,}76/n^2\) µJ. The factor 12 between the estimate and the actual error has two sources: point 1 of the lemma is twice too large (the actual largest derivative of the error is \(u''\,h/2\)), which is a factor 4 in the square, and the estimate takes the largest value instead of the mean square, which is \(u''\,h/\sqrt{12}\) against \(u''\,h/2\), a further factor 3. Together \(4 \cdot 3 = 12\). The estimate is therefore reliable but loose by a constant factor, while the order \(h^2\) is exact.

Hence step 2 of the proof of theorem 6.41 is here an equality. The estimate (6.26) holds for each mesh separately, also for the meshes with 2 and 3 elements, which are not one inside the other and about which theorem 6.35 says nothing (section 6.4.5).

Now we have three solid statements for the Ritz method. The error is orthogonal to the trial fields and the Ritz field is the best in the energy norm (lemma 6.36 and theorem 6.37, shown by linearity and positivity of the energy). The displacement at a point is exact when the field of the unit force lies in the family (theorem 6.38, shown by the work of the unit force and orthogonality). For a piecewise linear family the error falls as \(h^2\) in energy (theorem 6.41, shown by interpolation and Rolle's theorem). What remains is the question of what to do where there is no energy, and the answer is in the next section.

6.6 Galerkin method and weighted residuals (Galerkinova metoda in uteženi ostanki)

The Ritz method of section 6.4 chooses the numbers \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\) so that the total potential energy is smallest. For this it needs an energy. The weak form (šibka oblika) of section 6.1.2, however, is an equation that holds for every test function (preizkusna funkcija) and does not mention energy. Can we look for an approximation directly from it? And while we are at it: in how many ways can we demand that the error of an approximation be small, and how do these ways differ?

We look for the answer on the hanging bar that we know from chapter 4 and section 6.4.2. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m, cross-sectional area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and modulus of elasticity \(E = 196\) GPa is fixed at \(x = 0\), the axis \(x\) points downward, and the lower end is free. It is loaded by its own weight \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m per unit length, \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N. The true field is \(u = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), the lower end moves by \(19{,}52\) µm and the middle by \(14{,}64\) µm. The trial field (poskusno polje) throughout this section is the cubic function

\[u_1(x) = c\,\psi(x) , \qquad \psi(x) = 3L^2 x - x^3 . \tag{6.27}\]

We chose it because it respects the fixing, \(\psi(0) = 0\), and because \(\psi'(L) = 3(L^2 - L^2) = 0\), so the field has zero axial force at the free end, as the true field has. The second derivative \(\psi'' = -6x\) is not zero, so we will also be able to try the ways that need a second derivative. And the true function is not among the fields \(c\,\psi\), because it is quadratic and \(\psi\) is cubic, so the ways will give different results. Here \(c\) is a number with the unit \(\text{m}^{-2}\), since \(\psi\) is in \(\text{m}^3\) and \(u_1\) in m.

6.6.1 Galerkin method (Galerkinova metoda)

The true solution \(u\) satisfies the weak form, \(B(u, w) = \ell(w)\), for every test function \(w\) (definition 6.6). The trial field \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) cannot satisfy it for all \(w\), since it would otherwise be the true field. But we can satisfy it for \(n\) test functions, as many as there are unknown numbers. Which ones should they be? The simplest choice is to take the very functions from which the trial field is built. Where this idea comes from is told in the next paragraph.

From history

Around the turn from the nineteenth to the twentieth century, Rayleigh, Ritz and Galerkin were among the prominent contributors to approximate variational methods (EP, pp. 3 to 4). Galerkin published his work in 1915 (EP, pp. 701 and 705). The work of Rayleigh and Ritz, together with Galerkin's weighted-residual approach, formed a consistent framework in which a continuous problem with infinitely many degrees of freedom is replaced by a discrete one (GR, PDF p. 354). In their original form these methods were not flexible enough for systems of complex geometry with arbitrary boundary conditions and loading (GR, PDF p. 354). Galerkin's idea is to make the residual of the differential equation orthogonal to the functions from which the approximation is built (EP, p. 344). The name is often used also for an expression in which integration by parts has reduced the order of the derivatives, but this turns Galerkin's original idea into the Ritz method (EP, p. 345). The method in which the weights are the same functions as in the approximation is called more precisely after Bubnov and Galerkin (COOK, PDF p. 196).

Let us return to the weak form of the bar. The equation \(B(u, w) = \ell(w)\) must be true for every test function. Which test functions do we take once we restrict the trial field to the family \(\psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) (definition 6.32)? Galerkin's answer is this.

Definition 6.42 Galerkin method (Galerkinova metoda)

Let the problem be written in the weak form \(B(u, w) = \ell(w)\) for every test function \(w\), with a bilinear form \(B\) and a linear form \(\ell\) (definition 6.6). Let \(\psi_0\) be an admissible field, \(\psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) independent test functions and \(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) the set of all their linear combinations (definition 6.32). The Galerkin approximation is a function \(u_{\mathrm{n}} \in \psi_0 + \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) for which

\[B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) = \ell(w) \quad \text{for every } w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}} . \tag{6.28}\]

The trial and the test functions are from the same family.

Source: EP (6.4.12), (6.4.13), p. 344, COOK §5.1, PDF pp. 193 to 196 ("a Galerkin statement incorporates differential equations in their weak form", PDF p. 193).

How many equations is this? The demand holds for each of infinitely many fields \(w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\), but the equations for \(w = \psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) already suffice, and they are linear in the numbers \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Lemma 6.43 Galerkin equations (Galerkinove enačbe)

Let \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = \psi_0 + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} \psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) be as in definition 6.42. Then equation (6.28) holds for every \(w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) exactly when \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\). These equations are the system \(K\,c = f\) with \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) and \(f_{\mathrm{i}} = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}) - B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\).

Proof

We must show that the difference \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) - \ell(w)\) for each \(w\) splits into the differences for the functions \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\).

  1. Every \(w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) is \(w = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} d_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\). Since \(B\) is linear in the second argument and \(\ell\) is linear, \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, w) - \ell(w) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} d_{\mathrm{i}}\,\big(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) - \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\big)\).
  2. If all terms in the brackets are zero, then by step 1 the sum is zero for every choice of the numbers \(d_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the equation holds for every \(w\).
  3. If the equation holds for every \(w \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\), it also holds for \(w = \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\), since \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}} \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{n}}\) (\(d_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\), the other \(d\) zero). These are the equations \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\).
  4. Since \(B\) is linear in the first argument, \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\,B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\). The equation \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\,c_{\mathrm{j}} = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}) - B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\), row \(i\) of the system \(K\,c = f\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The same step is in the proof of lemma 6.36, steps 2 and 3.

The matrix \(K\) and the right-hand side \(f\) are the same as in the Ritz method (definition 6.32). The only difference is that in the Galerkin method \(B\) need not be symmetric, and therefore the matrix \(K\) need not be either.

A bar with the cubic field. Let us write out the definition for the field (6.27). The essential condition is \(u(0) = 0\), so \(\psi_0 = 0\), \(n = 1\), \(\psi_1 = \psi\), and equation (6.28) is \(B(c\,\psi, \psi) = \ell(\psi)\) with \(B(u, w) = \int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\ell(w) = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\). The numbers \(B(\psi, \psi) = \tfrac{24}{5}\,EA\,L^5\) and \(\ell(\psi) = \tfrac54\,q\,L^4\) are the matrix and the right side of the Ritz equation of section 6.4.2, so the Galerkin equation \(\tfrac{24}{5}\,EA\,L^5\,c = \tfrac54\,q\,L^4\) is the same and gives \(c = \tfrac{25}{96}\,q/(EA\,L)\). The field has \(20{,}33\) µm at the end, \(4{,}2\ \%\) too much, and \(13{,}98\) µm in the middle, \(4{,}5\ \%\) too little, while the work of the weight is \(2{,}3\ \%\) smaller than the true one, as theorem 6.34 says (section 6.4.4). By the weak form for \(u\) and the Galerkin equation, \(B(u - u_1, \psi) = \ell(\psi) - B(u_1, \psi) = 0\) (lemma 6.36), so the error is orthogonal to \(\psi\) in the energy inner product.

Is this a coincidence? For a bar \(B\) is symmetric, and the two methods coincide for every symmetric \(B\).

Theorem 6.44 Galerkin and Ritz methods coincide (Galerkinova in Ritzova metoda sovpadata)

Let \(B\) be a symmetric bilinear form, \(B(v, w) = B(w, v)\) for all admissible \(v\), \(w\), let \(\ell\) be a linear form and \(\Pi(w) = \tfrac12\,B(w, w) - \ell(w)\) the total potential energy. Let \(\psi_0, \psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the functions of definition 6.32. Then the Galerkin equations \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}})\) for \(k = 1, \dots, n\) are exactly the equations \(\partial \Pi/\partial c_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) of the Ritz method, that is, the same system \(K\,c = f\) with the same solution \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\).

Proof

We must show that the derivative of the energy with respect to \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals the Galerkin expression.

  1. Let \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = \psi_0 + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} \psi_{\mathrm{j}}\). By bilinearity and symmetry, \(B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_0) = B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{j}})\), we have \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, u_{\mathrm{n}}) = B(\psi_0, \psi_0) + 2\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{j}}) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\).
  2. By linearity of \(\ell\), \(\ell(u_{\mathrm{n}}) = \ell(\psi_0) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\,\ell(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})\). The energy \(\Pi\) is therefore a polynomial of second order in \(c_1, \dots, c_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  3. The term \(c_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\) has the derivative \(\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,c_{\mathrm{j}} + c_{\mathrm{i}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\) with respect to \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) (product rule). Hence the derivative of the double sum is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{i}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}})\), which by symmetry is \(2\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}})\).
  4. From steps 1 to 3, \(\dfrac{\partial \Pi}{\partial c_{\mathrm{k}}} = \tfrac12\,\big(2B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) + 2\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}})\big) - \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}) = B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) - \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}})\), where the derivative of \(\ell(u_{\mathrm{n}})\) with respect to \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}})\), was taken from step 2 and the last equality follows from bilinearity.
  5. By step 4 and lemma 6.43, \(\partial \Pi/\partial c_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{kj}}\,c_{\mathrm{j}} - f_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(K_{\mathrm{kj}} = B(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}})\) and \(f_{\mathrm{k}} = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}) - B(\psi_0, \psi_{\mathrm{k}})\). The Ritz method takes the numbers \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) from \(K\,c = f\) (definition 6.32), that is, from the condition \(\partial \Pi/\partial c_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) for every \(k\), as it must be at the lowest point (section 4.6.6). By step 4 the same condition is \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{k}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{k}})\) for every \(k\), and by lemma 6.43 these are the Galerkin equations.

Source: EP p. 345 ("The Ritz and Galerkin methods yield the same set of algebraic equations for the following three cases"), COOK §5.1, PDF p. 196 (the same for the choice of the same family). The proof is not from a source.

We have shown that the Galerkin equations are the condition that the derivative of the energy with respect to each \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero, written with the bilinear form and work instead of a derivative. For the bar with the cubic field this can be seen: \(\Pi(c) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{24}{5}\,EA L^5 c^2 - \tfrac54\,qL^4 c\) has the derivative \(\tfrac{24}{5}\,EA L^5 c - \tfrac54\,qL^4\), which is the Galerkin equation above. The Ritz calculation in section 6.4.2 and the Galerkin calculation above have the same number, \(c = 25/96\ q/(EAL)\), and the energy \(\Pi = -381{,}87\) µJ.

Why then do we need a new name at all? Because the Galerkin method does not need an energy. The bilinear form \(B\) and the right-hand side \(\ell\) of the weak form are enough. In some problems, for example in fluid flows, we have only a differential equation and boundary conditions, and a functional similar to the potential energy cannot be written or has no clear physical meaning (COOK, PDF p. 193). Then we write the weak form from the equation itself, as COOK (PDF pp. 194 to 195) does for a bar, and as a nonstructural example it names steady heat conduction (COOK, PDF p. 194), to which chapter 14 is devoted. The Galerkin method works there, the Ritz method does not. Also most of what we proved for the Ritz method in section 6.5 remains. The proof of lemma 6.36 uses only the weak form for \(u\) (step 1) and the equations \(K\,c = f\) (steps 2 and 3), which by lemma 6.43 are the Galerkin equations, and it does not need symmetry, so it holds for every \(B\) and every Galerkin approximation. The steps of the proof of theorem 6.39 for the constant \(M/m\) use only this orthogonality and the estimates \(|B(v, w)| \le M \int |v'|\,|w'|\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(B(w, w) \ge m \int w'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), and they do not need symmetry either. Hence the same steps give Cea's estimate with the constant \(M/m\) also for an unsymmetric \(B\) that has these two estimates. The estimate with the constant \(\sqrt{M/m}\) and theorem 6.37, however, need symmetry, because the splitting \(B(e + d, e + d) = B(e, e) + 2B(e, d) + B(d, d)\) in the proof of theorem 6.37 combines two mixed terms into \(2B(e, d)\). We do not develop unsymmetric problems further, since the book does not need them in this chapter.

6.6.2 Weighted residuals (uteženi ostanki)

The Galerkin method is the weak form with a particular choice of test functions. But what if we take the differential equation directly, without integration by parts? We insert the trial field into the equilibrium equation of the bar, and how much the equation fails is told by the residual.

Definition 6.45 Residual of a trial field (ostanek poskusnega polja)

Let a bar with axial stiffness \(EA\) and axial load \(q\) be as in definition 6.1, and let \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) be a trial field for which \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'\) is a differentiable function. The residual of the trial field is the function

\[R(x) = \big(EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'(x)\big)' + q(x) , \tag{6.29}\]

a number with the unit N/m at every point \(x \in [0, L]\). The residual is zero at every point exactly when the field satisfies the differential equation of equilibrium.

Source: EP (6.4.3), (6.4.5), pp. 338 and 340, COOK (5.1-2), PDF p. 194.

For the field (6.27) we compute the residual in three steps.

  1. The derivative is \(u_1' = 3c\,(L^2 - x^2)\).
  2. The axial force \(EA\,u_1' = 3c\,EA\,(L^2 - x^2)\) has the derivative \(-6c\,EA\,x\).
  3. The residual is \(R(x) = q - 6c\,EA\,x\), a straight line in \(x\) that equals the load \(q\) at \(x = 0\) and falls with a slope determined by \(c\).

The residual cannot be zero everywhere: that would require \(q = 6c\,EA\,x\) for every \(x\), which holds for no \(c\). We must demand something weaker. We choose \(n\) functions and demand that the residual be orthogonal to them, which means that the integral of the product is zero (inner product of functions, definition 6.16).

Definition 6.46 Weighted-residual method (metoda uteženih ostankov)

Let \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = \psi_0 + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} \psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) be a trial field of a bar with the residual \(R\) (definition 6.45) that meets the essential conditions and the natural condition \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'(L) = F\). Let \(w_1, \dots, w_{\mathrm{n}}\) be independent continuous functions on \([0, L]\), the weight functions (utežne funkcije), which may differ from the \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\). The weighted-residual method determines the numbers \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) from the \(n\) equations

\[\int_0^L R(x)\,w_{\mathrm{i}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 , \qquad i = 1, \dots, n . \tag{6.30}\]

If the trial field does not meet the natural condition, the residual at the boundary must be added to the equations.

Source: EP §6.4.2, (6.4.4) to (6.4.6), pp. 339 to 340 ("which, in general, are different from the approximation functions", p. 340), COOK §5.2, PDF pp. 196 to 197.

For a linear problem the equations (6.30) are linear in \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\), just like the Galerkin ones. We wrote the method for a bar, for a general differential equation it is written by EP (6.4.4) to (6.4.6). Why must the trial field also meet the natural condition? In the weak form this condition is already in the equation, in the equation with the residual it is not (EP, pp. 340 to 341), so the field itself must ensure it. The field (6.27) meets it, since \(u_1'(L) = c\,\psi'(L) = 0\) and \(F = 0\).

The methods differ in the choice of the weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}}\) (EP (6.4.11), p. 341).

  1. Galerkin, \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\). The residual must be orthogonal to the trial functions themselves.
  2. Petrov-Galerkin, the weights are functions other than \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\), for example \(w_1 = x\). We separate the families of trial and test functions (EP, p. 270, example 6.4.1, pp. 342 to 344, COOK PDF p. 196). With the weight \(x\) we will obtain below the exact displacement of the end.
  3. Least squares (najmanjši kvadrati): we minimize \(I(c) = \int_0^L R^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). The derivative \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}c_{\mathrm{i}}} = 2\int_0^L R\,\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial c_{\mathrm{i}}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) must be zero at the minimum, so the residual is orthogonal to \(\partial R/\partial c_{\mathrm{i}}\). This is the weighted-residual method with the weight \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \partial R/\partial c_{\mathrm{i}}\) (EP §6.4.4, (6.4.14) to (6.4.18), p. 349, COOK (5.2-4), (5.2-5), PDF p. 197). EP also adds to the functional a term with the boundary residual, which we omit because our field meets the natural condition (EP, pp. 349 to 350).
  4. Collocation (kolokacija): the residual is zero at chosen points, \(R(x_{\mathrm{i}}) = 0\) (COOK, PDF p. 197, EP §6.4.5, p. 356). The weight is concentrated at the point \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\). EP (6.4.29) writes it with the Dirac delta, a function concentrated at a point, which we will not need.
  5. Subdomain (podobmočje): we divide the bar into parts \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) and demand that the integral of the residual over each part is zero, \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{i}}} R\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). The weight is \(1\) on this part and \(0\) elsewhere (EP §6.4.6, (6.4.34) to (6.4.36), pp. 358 to 359, COOK PDF p. 197).

With the Galerkin choice the connection with the weak form appears. With integration by parts from chapter 3 we can turn the residual with the weight \(\psi\) into the weak form.

Lemma 6.47 Weighted residual and weak form (utežni ostanek in šibka oblika)

Let a bar with axial stiffness \(EA\) that is continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\) be fixed at \(x = 0\), loaded by a continuous axial load \(q\) and by a force \(F\) at the end \(x = L\). Let \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) be a field with a continuous second derivative, \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'(L) = F\), and \(\psi\) a continuously differentiable function with \(\psi(0) = 0\). Then

\[\int_0^L R\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = \ell(\psi) - B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi) , \tag{6.31}\]

where \(B(u, w) = \int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\ell(w) = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L)\).

Proof

We must show that integration by parts turns the residual into the weak form.

  1. By the definition of the residual, \(\int_0^L R\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L (EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}')'\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L q\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. The functions \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'\) and \(\psi\) are continuously differentiable, so by corollary 3.41 \(\int_0^L (EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}')'\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'\,\psi\big]_0^L - \int_0^L EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'\,\psi'\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. At \(x = 0\) we have \(\psi(0) = 0\), at \(x = L\) we have \(EA\,u_{\mathrm{n}}'(L) = F\), so the square bracket equals \(F\,\psi(L)\).
  4. From steps 1 to 3, \(\int_0^L R\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = F\,\psi(L) - B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi) + \int_0^L q\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = \ell(\psi) - B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi)\).

Source: COOK §5.1, (5.1-5) to (5.1-7), PDF pp. 194 to 195 (the same step). The proof in steps is not from the source.

We have shown that the equation with the weight \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is exactly the Galerkin equation \(B(u_{\mathrm{n}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = \ell(\psi_{\mathrm{i}})\) when the field meets the natural condition. The Galerkin method as EP (p. 344) describes it and its weak form therefore give the same, the difference is only whether we have already carried out the integration by parts. In the first form the field must have a second derivative and meet the natural condition, in the second a first derivative and the essential condition are enough.

Let us also compute the equations for the field (6.27). The residual of step 3 is \(R = q - 6c\,EA\,x\), its derivative with respect to \(c\) is \(\partial R/\partial c = -6\,EA\,x\).

  1. Galerkin: \(\int_0^L R\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac54\,qL^4 - 6c\,EA\,\int_0^L x\,(3L^2 x - x^3)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac54\,qL^4 - \tfrac{24}{5}\,c\,EA\,L^5\), because \(\int_0^L (3L^2 x^2 - x^4)\,\mathrm{d}x = L^5\,(1 - \tfrac15)\). The equation gives \(c = \tfrac{25}{96}\,q/(EA\,L)\), which by lemma 6.47 is the same number as for the weak form.
  2. Petrov-Galerkin with \(w = x\) and least squares: \(\int_0^L R\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,qL^2 - 6c\,EA\,\tfrac13 L^3 = 0\) gives \(c = \tfrac14\,q/(EA\,L)\). The weight of least squares is \(-6\,EA\,x\), proportional to \(x\), so its equation is the same.
  3. Collocation at \(x_1 = L/2\): \(R(L/2) = q - 3c\,EA\,L = 0\) gives \(c = \tfrac13\,q/(EA\,L)\).
  4. Subdomain, one whole bar \([0, L]\): \(\int_0^L R\,\mathrm{d}x = qL - 3c\,EA\,L^2 = 0\) gives \(c = \tfrac13\,q/(EA\,L)\).

Figure 6.22 shows the residuals for the obtained numbers and the weights that gave them. All the residuals are straight lines that start at \(R = q\) at \(x = 0\). With collocation the residual is zero in the middle of the bar and \(-q\) at the end, so by absolute value it is largest there. With Galerkin, \(R(L/2) = \tfrac{7}{32}\,q = 1{,}315\) N/m and \(R(L) = -\tfrac{9}{16}\,q\). The residual is zero only at \(x = \tfrac{16}{25}\,L = 6{,}4\) m, but the integral of its product with \(\psi\) is zero, and Galerkin demands no more.

What about the field from the chapter on energy? In section 4.6.8 we took \(u = c\,x\) and with the energy obtained \(c = aL\) and the exact displacement of the end. Its residual is \(R = q = 6{,}010\) N/m for every \(c\), as we saw for the strong form in section 6.1.1. For a weight that is positive everywhere, such as \(\psi\), \(x\) or \(1\), \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x > 0\), so the equation cannot be solved for any \(c\). Moreover, the field does not meet the natural condition, \(EA\,u'(L) = EA\,c \ne 0\), which the weak form does not demand. The weighted-residual method gives nothing with this field, while the cubic field (6.27) has a nonzero second derivative and is therefore suitable. In the methods with a residual the trial field must have a second derivative that can follow the equation, while the weak form needs only the first, which EP (p. 323) describes for the weak form as "weaker (i.e., lesser) differentiability".

6.6.3 Comparison of the methods (primerjava metod)

Which of the ways is best? The answer depends on what we measure. Let us compare them on the trial field (6.27), which separates them. The table gives the number \(c\) in units of \(q/(EA\,L)\), the displacement of the lower end and of the middle, and the energy of the error, which is \(\Pi(u_1) - \Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,\|u - u_1\|_{\mathrm{E}}^2\) by corollary 4.93, and the total energy \(\Pi\) (true field: \(\Pi = -391{,}03\) µJ, end \(19{,}52\) µm, middle \(14{,}64\) µm).

method \(c\) end µm middle µm \(U\) of error µJ \(\Pi\) µJ
Galerkin (\(w = \psi\)) \(25/96\) \(20{,}33\) (\(+4{,}2\ \%\)) \(13{,}98\) (\(-4{,}5\ \%\)) \(9{,}165\) \(-381{,}87\)
least squares \(1/4\) \(19{,}52\) (exact) \(13{,}42\) (\(-8{,}3\ \%\)) \(9{,}776\) \(-381{,}25\)
Petrov-Galerkin, \(w = x\) \(1/4\) \(19{,}52\) (exact) \(13{,}42\) \(9{,}776\) \(-381{,}25\)
collocation at \(L/2\) \(1/3\) \(26{,}03\) (\(+33\ \%\)) \(17{,}89\) (\(+22\ \%\)) \(39{,}10\) \(-351{,}93\)
subdomain \([0, L]\) \(1/3\) \(26{,}03\) \(17{,}89\) \(39{,}10\) \(-351{,}93\)

Figure 6.23 shows the fields and the energies of the errors. The numbers differ for four reasons.

Galerkin has the smallest energy of the error. This is theorem 6.37: among all the fields \(c\,\psi\) the field with the Ritz and Galerkin number has the error with the smallest strain energy. For \(c = \kappa\,q/(EA\,L)\) the energy of the error is \(9{,}165 + 5631\,(\kappa - \tfrac{25}{96})^2\) µJ (the table in section 6.5.1), the second term being the energy of the difference from the Galerkin field. So collocation has an energy of error \(39{,}10/9{,}165 = 4{,}3\) times larger than Galerkin. The number \(1/3\) is \(7/96\) away from \(25/96\), the number \(1/4\) only \(1/96\), and the second term grows with the square of the distance, so for collocation it is \(49\) times larger than for least squares, \(29{,}94\) against \(0{,}611\) µJ.

Least squares and \(w = x\) give the exact displacement of the end. For the weight \(w = x\) we have \(w' = 1\), so \(B(u_1, x) = \int_0^L EA\,u_1'\,\mathrm{d}x = EA\,u_1(L)\), and \(\ell(x) = \int_0^L q\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,qL^2\). The equation \(\int_0^L R\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) is by lemma 6.47 (the field meets the natural condition, \(F = 0\)) equal to \(B(u_1, x) = \ell(x)\), so \(EA\,u_1(L) = \tfrac12\,qL^2\). The weak form with \(w = x\) says the same for the true field, so \(u_1(L) = u(L)\). This weight is \(EA\) times the field \(G = x/EA\), which is the field of a unit force at the end of the bar, and for every admissible field \(v\) we have \(B(G, v) = \int_0^L v'\,\mathrm{d}x = v(L)\), which is exactly the reason why the equation reads off the displacement of the end. In theorem 6.38 this is the field \(G_{\mathrm{L}}\), which must lie in the trial family for the displacement to be exact. In the Galerkin method the test family is the same as the trial family, so \(G_{\mathrm{L}}\) must lie in it, while in the Petrov-Galerkin method we choose the test function ourselves and choose \(x\). In least squares the weight is proportional to \(x\), because \(\partial R/\partial c = -6\,EA\,x\), and the equation is the same.

Collocation at \(L/2\) is the same as subdomain. The residual is a straight line, \(R = q - 6c\,EA\,x\). The mean of a straight line over an interval is its value in the middle, \(\int_0^L R\,\mathrm{d}x = L\,R(L/2)\), so the equations \(R(L/2) = 0\) and \(\int_0^L R\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) give the same number.

Which measure is the right one? The energy of the error is smallest for Galerkin. The displacement of the end is best for least squares. In the middle the error of Galerkin is \(-4{,}5\ \%\), of least squares \(-8{,}3\ \%\) and of collocation \(+22\ \%\). The theorem holds only for the energy: Galerkin is best in this sense for every trial space (theorem 6.37), while the exact displacement of the end in least squares is a consequence of the weight being proportional to \(x\), which is the field of the force at the end of the bar, and not a property of the method. If we were interested in the displacement of the middle, nothing of this would be guaranteed.

Matrices. In the Ritz method the matrix \(K\) is symmetric, because \(B\) is symmetric, and so it is in the Galerkin method with a symmetric \(B\) (theorem 6.44). In least squares the matrix \(\int_0^L (EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}')'\,(EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}')'\,\mathrm{d}x\) is symmetric already because of the commutativity of the product, and as a matrix of inner products of the functions \((EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}')'\) it is positive definite if these functions are independent (lemma 6.28). EP (p. 350) writes that this is "the only other method, in addition to the Ritz method, that is based on the minimization of a functional and results in a symmetric coefficient matrix". In collocation and Petrov-Galerkin the matrix is in general unsymmetric (EP, p. 340), and we do not have the positive definiteness that guarantees a single solution (theorem 6.29). For \(n = 1\) the matrix is \(1 \times 1\) and always symmetric, so our example cannot show this. In collocation the choice of points matters: EP (p. 358) shows that for a simply supported beam with two parameters the points \(L/4\) and \(3L/4\) give the same relations between the numbers \(c_1\) and \(c_2\), so no solution follows from them.

Finite differences (končne razlike). We can use collocation in one more way. We divide the bar into \(n\) equal parts of length \(h = L/n\) with grid points \(x_{\mathrm{i}} = i h\) and demand that the residual be zero at the points \(x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{n}}\). The unknowns are not coefficients of trial functions but the values \(u_{\mathrm{i}} \approx u(x_{\mathrm{i}})\), and the second derivative is replaced by a difference. The central quotient of section 2.7.4 gives \(u'(x_{\mathrm{i}} + h/2) \approx (u_{\mathrm{i}+1} - u_{\mathrm{i}})/h\) and \(u'(x_{\mathrm{i}} - h/2) \approx (u_{\mathrm{i}} - u_{\mathrm{i}-1})/h\), and with it applied to \(u'\) we obtain

\[u''(x_{\mathrm{i}}) \approx \frac{u'(x_{\mathrm{i}} + h/2) - u'(x_{\mathrm{i}} - h/2)}{h} \approx \frac{u_{\mathrm{i}+1} - 2u_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}-1}}{h^2} .\]

For constant \(EA\) the equation at the point \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) is then \(EA\,(u_{\mathrm{i}+1} - 2u_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}-1})/h^2 + q = 0\), at \(x_0 = 0\) we have \(u_0 = 0\), and the natural condition \(u'(L) = 0\) we write with the central quotient around \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\), \((u_{\mathrm{n}+1} - u_{\mathrm{n}-1})/(2h) = 0\), so \(u_{\mathrm{n}+1} = u_{\mathrm{n}-1}\) (the point \(x_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) is auxiliary, outside the bar). For \(n = 2\) and \(n = 4\) we solved the system with NumPy. We obtain exactly the true values: \(14{,}64\) and \(19{,}52\) µm for \(n = 2\), and \(8{,}540\), \(14{,}64\), \(18{,}30\) and \(19{,}52\) µm for \(n = 4\). Why exactly? The true field is quadratic, and the central quotient of a quadratic function is exact (section 2.7.4), so the true values satisfy the difference equations. The system has a single solution: the homogeneous system gives \(u_{\mathrm{i}+1} - 2u_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}-1} = 0\) for \(i < n\) and \(u_0 = 0\), so \(u_{\mathrm{i}} = i s\) for some number \(s\), and the last equation \(u_{\mathrm{n}-1} - u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) gives \(s = 0\). The exactness is therefore a consequence of the quadratic true field and not a property of the method, for other fields the central quotient is not exact and the values are not hit exactly. This paragraph is not from the sources. We do not treat the boundary element method (metoda robnih elementov) in the book.

The eigenvalues that the Ritz method looks for in vibration (the Rayleigh quotient) need mass and motion, so we treat them in chapter 13.

With this we have answered the two questions from the start of the section. We can use the weak form directly, without energy: the Galerkin method with the same functions for the trial and the test fields gives for a symmetric \(B\) the same equations as the Ritz method, and the orthogonality of the error and Cea's estimate hold. We can also make the error small with weighted residuals, and the five ways of choosing the weights give for the same cubic field an energy of error between \(9{,}165\) and \(39{,}10\) µJ. The theorem on the best approximation guarantees this only for the Galerkin choice, so the next section builds the trial fields from pieces of straight lines, which this theorem covers.

6.7 Piecewise linear trial fields

The Ritz method (section 6.4) finds the best field in a family of fields that we choose. For the hanging bar we built the family from polynomials that run over the whole length. This choice has two weaknesses. First, a single polynomial cannot have a kink, such as the displacement of a bar with a step in its cross section has (section 6.1.3), because a polynomial has a continuous derivative everywhere. Second, the functions \(x, x^2, \dots, x^n\) become more and more alike on the interval, so the system of equations for the coefficients becomes harder and harder to solve, as we saw in section 6.3. What happens if we cut the bar into pieces and take a straight line on each piece?

We will find the answer in four steps. First we look for the functions from which any continuous function made of straight pieces is built. With them we solve the hanging bar that we already know, and look at how wrong the approximation is. Then we apply the same idea to the bar with a step, where polynomials fail. Finally we show why the idea does not carry over to the beam.

6.7.1 Hat functions

The idea of taking the pieces separately did not arise with bars. Let us see how it arose and what it solved.

From history

The Rayleigh-Ritz method and Galerkin's weighted-residual approach reduced, according to GR (PDF p. 354), a problem with infinitely many degrees of freedom to a finite number of unknowns. In their original form, however, they lacked the flexibility that systems of complex shape with arbitrary boundary conditions and arbitrary load distribution demand (GR, PDF p. 354). According to COOK (PDF p. 170), the classical Rayleigh-Ritz method regarded the entire structure as a single domain and spanned it with a single trial function. According to GR (PDF p. 354), the era of finite elements formally started with a lecture by R. Courant in 1941.
